#4856. My Kid Wants to Play Grand Theft Auto. Now What?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

For the last days, even weeks, millions of parents have been fielding the pleas from their adolescent, even pre-adolescent, children to buy and play what is likely to be the biggest video game release in history – Grand Theft Auto VI.

Overall, it's important to have a balanced perspective. We don't need to get apocalyptic about this release. For most people, GTA6 will be a relatively harmless diversion that will consume a monstrous amount of time and then fade out. The risk that playing this game will turn your overall well-adjusted teen into a murderer or drug dealer is very low. This game, and media in general, is not the primary driver of mental health problems in youth; that would still be the old standbys: genetics, trauma, and adverse child experiences—social drivers of health.

The release of this game to child development and mental health professions is similar to how Halloween is experienced by dentists. Everything about it feels wrong, but few youth will probably experience long-term harm.

That said, we should not be naïve or complacent about some of the real risks.

These come in two main categories. The first is what is sometimes called displacement, which basically refers to the sheer volume of hours that youth will choose to spend on this game rather than on something healthier. Video games, just like gambling, are addictive, so some people are just not going to be able to stop and that can interfere with sleeping, homework, or just about anything else.

The second area of concern is related to the game’s content. GTA6 has everything that might be contained in an R-rated movie including graphic violence, drug and alcohol use and trafficking, nudity, and profanity. So, really, the question if you are a parent wondering about buying the game or letting your child get the game is: Would you be comfortable giving them unlimited and unsupervised access to being immersed in an interactive R-rated movie? I’ve heard they tried to dial down the misogynistic content in this version. We’ll see.

Even if the game doesn’t make your child act violently, it will still be tough to push out the more aggressive and misogynistic thoughts that will be swirling around in their head. There is also the concern that excessive exposure to violent video games can desensitize youth to real world violence.

Of course, adolescents are different and individuals are going to react differently to playing the game. For many it will be a relatively harmless waste of time but for others there could be more serious consequences, and it is important to try and see how playing the game affects your individual child.

Sometimes I wish I could be one of those cool adults who is totally chill with immersive content that glorifies violence and criminal behavior, but I guess I’m not. Good luck, parents.

#4854. The Customer Loyalty Secret? It’s Not Just About Shopping

Imagine you’re at home one morning—settled in, slippers on, cozy. Your kids are playing in the next room. A couple of miles away, your local Pottery Barn is hosting a bed-styling workshop: You’ll learn how to layer coverlets and quilts, mix patterns, and plan for seasonality. And maybe at the end of it, you’ll get a small discount for an in-store purchase.

Do you go? Or, do you hop onto YouTube or TikTok and search for “bed-styling ideas”—slippers still on? Maybe you find what you’re looking for on Pottery Barn’s own YouTube channel. Maybe you search for some quilts like those you saw in the video, and—what’s this? A similar-looking option for less, from another brand that isn’t Pottery Barn?

Getting people out of their slippers and into the store—again and again—is one challenge that pros like Evan Hutton, McGee & Co.’s head of retail store operations and a veteran of the industry, are taking seriously. “It used to be you could just do a bed-styling class or [a class on] how to decorate a mantel, and people would come for that,” she says. No longer: Thanks to YouTube tutorials, the lure has to be much more compelling. The promise of social and experiential elements like gelato carts or floral-arranging workshops give customers a social and sensory reason to show up, she says. This strategy for cultivating customer loyalty is already making its way into the first McGee & Co. flagship in Salt Lake City, which opened in September.

Retails are seeing a growing interest for hands-on events, like this keychain-making activity at McGee & Co.

Shea McGee's finished keychain, complete with a monogram.

“I think of in-store programming as retail theater,” says Geri Moran, vice president of marketing at ABC Carpet & Home, a longtime New York City home shopping mecca. The beauty of programming, she notes, is that it brings together “commerce, culture, and discovery.” Importantly, it doesn’t even need to produce a sale right away, either. “It can build awareness, strengthen relationships with the design community, introduce new customers to the store, and give existing customers another reason to return,” she says.

During the holiday season, ABC Carpet & Home hosts carolers at its NYC flagship as a way to “give [customers] a reason to visit, connect, and come back,” says Moran.

She points to a caroling event held at ABC during the holiday season. Those fa-la-las aren’t frivolous: They’re how ABC makes an emotional imprint on its community, even if it may have very little to do with a specific product. “The merchandise gives people a reason to shop,” she says, “but the experience gives them a reason to visit, connect, and come back.”

Another way to get people coming back? Introduce elements that can only be discovered in person, whether that’s through store design, specialty goods, or locally made wares. Across the industry, brands are tackling this in a few different ways. McGee & Co., for one, is planning to include regional variations on their signature design language across its outposts as they expand across the US. Syd McGee, the company’s CEO, imagines a McGee fan encountering the store in different cities, each location informed by local culture. How does McGee do Texas versus California? There’s only one way to find out, he says.

The business is also embracing the potential of merchandise that can only be purchased in-store. At the opening of their Salt Lake City flagship, McGee & Co. offered gardening gear, Cire Trudon candles, Match pewter, and vintage pieces only shoppable in person. Though customers may have initially come to the flagship to check out a new piece of furniture, they’ll discover that their local store can also be a resource for gifts and one-off finds from the McGee universe.

The Lawson-Fenning showroom creates a welcoming environment for clients.

Lawson-Fenning, a homeware brand that has built a reputation for California-inflected design, takes a similar approach to layering, blending their own collection with vintage they’ve found and work from makers they admire. “There’s always something they didn’t come in for,” says cofounder Grant Fenning, adding that “plenty of our longtime clients first walked in without a plan.” While much of their consumer base encounters the brand for the first time through a designer, shoppers will often return on their own a year or two later.

A retailer’s job isn’t just to showcase hero products—it’s to build a world. Which might be why Il Buco Vita, a lifestyle brand offshoot of Il Buco’s hospitality business, does around 60 percent of its business in person, despite having a website full of products. Founder Donna Lennard notes that art, antiques, and decorative pieces frequently sell more in store, while online sales skew toward more everyday kitchen and dining products. “It all comes down to keeping the discovery process interesting,” says Lennard. “With each person that walks through the door, there is an opportunity to introduce them to something they might not have known they were looking for,” she says.

The associates working the showroom floor help complete the picture, educating customers about the artisans, product pairings, and long-term care of pieces. But this year, Il Buco Vita is taking their world-building efforts one step further by opening a new retail flagship on Bond Street, just a few doors down from their original restaurant. This proximity, Lennard says, “creates a stronger connection between hospitality and home,” and provides a setting to present larger pieces, antiques, and collections in a more experiential atmosphere. “Customers can see how they live together and imagine them in their own homes.”

Every issue, every era. Explore 100+ years of the Architectural Digest Archive, an unparalleled digital resource for research and inspiration. Start Searching

Across the board, the brands interviewed for this story identified trust as the key ingredient in creating repeat customers. Cultivating it begins from the moment someone begins engaging with your team—and it doesn’t end when the credit card swipes. “The sale isn’t truly complete when the customer pays,” Moran says. “It’s complete when the product has arrived, the customer is happy with it, and the experience makes them want to return.”

Associates’ product knowledge is the first half of the equation. Customers depend on sales staff to understand not just a product, but the whole-room experience that brands can deliver. This expertise also supports conversations on pricing. In the showroom, customers can test-drive a sofa, run their fingers across different types of upholstery, and scrutinize construction alongside an associate, who can help them unpack the differences between two similar models. “The conversation then becomes less about price and more about value, craftsmanship, longevity, and whether the product is right for the customer,” says Moran. “Our team can also help identify alternatives when something isn’t the right fit for a customer’s budget.”

Hutton notes that for McGee & Co., there was a deliberate decision made to refer to in-store employees as “design associates.” “When a customer comes in, we don’t want it to be, ‘Oh, let me take you over to the design concierge,’” says Hutton. “We want all our team members to be able to start those conversations—and oftentimes finish them too.”

Shea McGee, who briefed many of those first-time flagship associates herself, notes that education on the product forms a significant part of their training. The goal is for trainees to understand showroom furniture from the perspective of a designer, and to be able to translate that to the customer. By doing so, she says, associates will help buyers “make that connection between ‘designer led’ and our brand.”

Studio McGee's senior-level designers host regular check-ins with McGee & Co.’s design associates to help bridge the brand's designer-led vision.

For trade-focused businesses, trust-building exists outside of a single transaction. Tyla Caccese, the founder of the 15-year-old trade-only rug company Tailor-Made Textiles, emphasizes a practical tack. For her new 2,000-square-foot showroom in Manhattan, “We wanted it to feel more like a workshop,” she says. The design followed: There’s a big marble kitchen island where designers can spread out drawings, plug in their laptops, or work through a project over lunch.

This thinking was informed by her experiences in a shared space her brand occupied previously, where she noticed remote-working designers using the showroom as a kind of third place—not quite a home, not quite an office. “It’s been wonderful to see designers using the showroom almost as an extension of their own studios,” she says. These current and prospective customers can get to know and trust the brand through proximity and natural conversation, turning to Caccese to work through ideas and feel at home, whether or not they’re there to source a rug. “I don’t want designers to feel like they need a project or a purchase order to come through the door,” she says. Showing that you can help them solve their problems is what will earn you their business. “Ultimately, what brings designers back isn’t necessarily a particular rug. It’s knowing they can walk in with an idea, a problem, or a completely unrealistic deadline and have a real conversation about how to make something work.”

Once a customer makes a purchase, overcommunicate, overcommunicate, overcommunicate, says Lawson-Fenning co-founder Glenn Lawson. He says that wait times are the biggest challenge facing their business, which makes all their furniture to order. A piece can take 10 or 12 weeks to produce—and for a designer working toward an install date, that matters. “We’d rather give a realistic date and hit it than promise something faster and miss,” says Lawson. “When people know where their piece is, the wait feels shorter.” And in a pinch, those only-in-store items can help too: Never underestimate the power of a floor sample.

At the new ABC Carpet & Home store in Boca Raton, Florida, customers can explore the brand's floor coverings in a range of settings, from residential vignettes to more gallery-like arrangements.

Ultimately, retailers need to recognize that in 2026 and beyond, you’re no longer just a merchant—you’re a builder of relationships. That kinship builds through events that cultivate brand affinity, solving customers’ problems together, and delivering compelling, can’t-find-it-elsewhere in-store discovery. But nurturing that connection is just as important as making it in the first place.

“It’s not uncommon for our top buyers to receive a personal email from our sales team, letting them know about what we have coming up next and personally inviting them to check out new collections,” says Lennard. Fenning seconds the motion: “Designers hear about new work first,” he says. “We invite them in for a new collection or a maker’s show. And when a project wraps, we want to see the photos.” The transaction might end at the register—but the relationship doesn’t have to.

#4852. The Healthiest Thing You Can Do for Your Prostate at Age 50

A lifesaving blood test just got a huge endorsement.

Prostate cancer is the second leading cause of cancer deaths in men, so you’d think doctors would be adamant about screening guys for it. Yet for years, prostate cancer screening via the PSA (prostate-specific antigen) test has been plagued by vague recommendations, and some back-and-forth messaging that flipped between “get it” and “the benefits might not be worth it.” Until recently, organizations including the American Cancer Society (ACS) used to give a recommendation that at age 50, guys should talk with their doctors about screening, then engage in a process of “shared decision-making” about whether to get the test.

Many guys didn’t know whether they should get it or not. Without a clear recommendation, it was easy for some to think this PSA blood test wasn’t very important to do at all. The landscape has changed.

The American Cancer Society just came out with new guidelines that for the first time, unequivocally say that men should get the screening test. Guys at average risk should start at age 50. Guys at higher risk (more on that later) should start at 45.

Why that’s a big deal: “The new guideline not only gets rid of shared decision-making, which is really difficult to execute, is subject to bias, and is really time-intensive,” says Yaw Nyame, MD, of the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center at the University of Washington Medical Center. “But it couples that with a better understanding of what present-day prostate cancer screening is.”

Today, the PSA test is “just the first step, not the final answer,” says William Dahut, MD, chief scientific officer at ACS, and a contributing author to the guidelines. “It is a simple blood test, and an elevated result does not automatically mean cancer of the need for a biopsy.” Many more tools including MRIs and biomarkers help physicians drill down on who needs additional testing. “Our goal is to find prostate cancer earlier, while avoiding unnecessary procedures and treatment,” Dr. Dahut adds.

What changed that prompted the revised recommendations? “It’s important to understand that guidance evolves as the evidence does,” says Dr. Dahut. Research has piled up to indicate that PSA screening reduces prostate cancer deaths.

“We do not need to make a disclaimer that maybe you should, maybe you shouldn’t do it. Everyone should do it and you should start early, especially if you have a higher risk of cancer,” says Dr. Nyame, who was on the expert panel that reviewed the new ACS screening guidelines.

While all men should get the test, according to the new guidelines, it’s not a “one size fits all” screening recommendation, Dr. Nyame explains. Recommendations vary according to risk. Find your category and screen according to that.

These are the new ACS guidelines for who and when:

Other prostate screening guidelines came out earlier in 2026 from the American Urological Association (AUA) and the Society for Urologic Oncology (SUO) that had slightly different recommendations for the age at which you should start screening. What gives? The difference in recommended age and frequency of screening “has to do with how the guideline creators are viewing the different studies that they’re using to support their decision making,” Dr. Nyame says.

It doesn’t mean guys should throw up their hands and do nothing in frustration. “The AUA/SUO and ACS guidelines recognize the benefit of knowing a PSA test result earlier in life. A PSA test in the 40- to 50-year age range is a good predictor of the likelihood someone has or will develop a clinically significant prostate cancer,” says James A. Eastham, MD, chief of the urology service, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. A higher level early in life is a strong signal that you need to be really diligent about checking your PSA.

“We’ve watched prostate cancer incidence increase—especially metastatic cancer, for over a decade now,” says Dr. Nyame. “And to know that we have a guideline that is so action-oriented toward reversing that course is really exciting.”

Marty Munson, currently the health director of Men's Health, has been a health editor at properties including Marie Claire, Prevention, Shape and RealAge. She's also certified as a swim and triathlon coach.

#4850. After Launching McGee & Co., Shea McGee Shares 8 Lessons for Opening a Store

My husband Syd and I are both lovers of retail, and have always known one day we’d have a McGee & Co. shop of our own. Over the years, we’ve spent a lot of time jotting down ideas for our own store. Our new flagship is a repository for all that knowledge that we’ve been squirreling away—but it also taught us a few lessons of its own.

Speaking to you now, on the other side of its debut, there are some things we only learned through actually doing. From the importance of developing a training manual to the do-or-die value of a soft launch, here are eight hard-won learnings from our McGee & Co. store launch.

It was important to us that the shop feel like the homes we create for our clients—layered and collected, with a variety of patterns and objects for your eye to explore. Despite the fact that the dollars-per-square-foot model is the traditional method of conceiving an in-store assortment, it was more important for us to remain true to ourselves with this first location: we’re a designer-led brand, not a merchant-led one.

“I’m getting to see our products through new eyes—and I was the one that concepted them!” says Shea. “When you see them in a store setting, pieces can have a lot more detail than you can see online.”

We started by coming up with the sections we envisioned, like a kids’ area, a kitchen zone, and so on. Then we created planograms to see how much we could actually fit, and reconciled with our merchandising team to see what made business sense. Sometimes, that meant pivoting from the early vision. A lighting gallery we had planned, for instance, ended up shifting: We loved the idea, but when we looked at the percentage of lighting to the rest of our sales, we could see clearly that it was a smarter business decision to use this space to showcase more furniture. Instead of the sprawling lighting gallery we had imagined, we created a moody lounge area that can flex to showcase different pieces.

We don’t think small: Our aspirations are to grow nationwide. But however much we scale, it’s critical that we not lose the warm, personal feeling that comes from a standalone store. As McGee & Co. grows its brick-and-mortar operation, that’s one of my biggest goals. And there’s another layer here, too: Being a personality-led business, the team members in our store aren’t just representing our brand—they’re representing me, for better or worse. The design world can sometimes feel closed-off and unapproachable, and it’s always been the McGee mantra—in our content, in our personality on social media, in how we work with clients—to be warm and accessible. Now that attitude needs to trickle down to our store associates, too.

Before we opened, I spent months developing a comprehensive training guide for our associates. It’s essentially Design 101, McGee-style, covering everything from how many inches I place a rug away from a wall, to how to pair and arrange accent tables, to how to layer bedding. We cover every level of the decorating process. Thank goodness for AI—it’s been a lifesaver: I’ll narrate as we go on our walk-throughs, and use those notes as the basis for the training manual. And it’s not a one-and-done deal. We’ll continue to add to this document as we evolve and grow.

Every issue, every era. Explore 100+ years of the Architectural Digest Archive, an unparalleled digital resource for research and inspiration. Start Searching

Having that Design 101 established is a first step, but how do you ensure that the team is really internalizing the lessons? For us, the answer was checkpoints. As our design associates go through training and familiarize themselves with our ways of doing things, we hold check-ins with them to make sure that they’re absorbing our ways of operating. It’s the exact same as we do for the junior interior designers at Studio McGee: The checkpoints allow us to build up mutual confidence, with the aim for them to eventually fly on their own.

Shea plans to have the studio’s senior-level designers hosting regular check-ins with the shop’s design associates.

Personally dropping in myself can serve as another kind of checkpoint, too. With the flagship local, I’m able to stop by regularly in these early days to make sure that our standards are upheld, that our visuals are tight, and the operation is humming. That won’t work for us in every location, but it’s certainly a perk of opening up in our own hometown.

As much as I love a good plan, there’s nothing like real-time feedback to show you what’s working and what’s not. Which is why we kicked off our flagship back in September with a whisper and not a bang. We did a very soft launch with no announcement, no social post. We just opened the doors. As folks wandered in, we learned, and we tweaked. And two weeks later, we opened officially. That soft-launch period was vital for us in getting the kinks out.

One benefit of having had an ecommerce business for so long is that we have rich data on exactly where our customers are. That means that from day one, we already know where we need to open next. While launching in Salt Lake City was a logical place for our flagship, we’re already thinking ahead to how we’ll expand to some of our other biggest markets, like Texas and California.

Located in Salt Lake City’s Trolley Square, the “shop,” as Shea calls it, is 7,500 square feet.

We want to capitalize on the fact that the retail-ecommerce loop is an advantageous cycle: Where you have a retail store, your ecommerce sales lift. People who are aware of your product can go see it in person, give it a sit test, think about it, and then finish the sale online. In store, we can educate them, give them styling suggestions, and show off the quality of the product in ways we can’t online. Even for us, we’re discovering new things about our assortment by merchandising it in the store—we’re seeing it with fresh eyes, and we know our customers will too.

Aside from the obvious metric of profitability, to me, success in these early days means nailing down our systems and processes. It’s not the most glamorous side of this business, but it’s a must. I want to be able to say that we know what it takes to run a store and to make the shopper experience in it as smooth as possible. For instance, I want customers to know how to get to our free design services, and to have a great experience using them. If we can do that, we know we’re on our way to some of our loftier goals, too.

I’m not under any illusions here: This first store is a baptism by fire. Not only are we opening a flagship and planting seeds for our future locations—we’re also doing it in Q4, right before the holidays. But my hope is that at the end of it, we can catch our breath and take a moment to reflect on what worked, what didn’t, and then get to work fixing it. In this business, honesty with yourself is the only way up.

“The kitchen is a working kitchen,” says Shea, who envisions cooking demos and community events enlivening the space.

#4847. How to Open a Retail Store, Win Customers, and Build a Business That Lasts

Even in the age of one-click shopping, opening an actual brick-and-mortar retail store is a dream for many designers. There’s something almost romantic about creating an entire environment where customers can sit on the sofas, feel the fabrics, or pick up a last-minute gift on their way to a party. It’s an opportunity to bring your brand to life and connect with customers in a way a website never can.

But opening a store requires a big leap of faith. Even if you have a loyal customer base, there’s something different about building a store. You have to think about everything from foot traffic to merchandising to hiring staff, and much more.

These are questions I’ve been wrestling with myself. Almost two months ago, after years of nurturing a thriving e-commerce business, my husband Syd and I unveiled our McGee & Co. flagship in our homebase of Salt Lake City. This project has been a goal of ours for a long time. We’ve been collecting ideas for years to ensure that whenever it opened, our physical retail operation would hold up to the high standards of service and design that we expect from every other part of our business. This project has had me thinking about retail at every hour of the day, mulling over some big questions... How do we translate a digital brand into a physical space for selling? How do we nurture customers and ensure they return? And how do we map our knowledge so that we can repeat our successes as we scale?

This guide, produced with our friends at AD PRO, distills some of the wisdom from our own experiences, as well as from a few insiders elsewhere in the industry. I’ll share some of the thinking and practical decisions behind our shop, from our merchandising strategy to how we recruited and trained our employees.

Next, AD PRO contributor Lila Allen speaks to me and my team, as well as professionals from retailers like Lawson-Fenning, Il Buco Vita, Tailor-Made Textiles, and ABC Carpet & Home, about how they cultivate customer loyalty over the long term. When access to product and knowledge is seemingly unlimited across the internet, we all agree: Earning trust and becoming a destination for discovery takes a lot of care. But it pays off. Relationships might be the most precious resource we have.

Then, contributor Margaret Borden catches up with the creatives behind some of this year’s buzziest shops—from a jewel-box fashion boutique in Paris to a bright, inviting kitchen and home goods shop in New York City—to glean their merchandising tips and tricks.

Whether you’re a designer thinking about hanging your own retail shingle, or you’re simply looking for a fresh perspective on the landscape of selling in 2026 and beyond, I hope this report will give you plenty of inspiration for the year ahead.

Our Salt Lake City flagship is a baptism by fire—but we wouldn’t have it any other way. Here’s how we planned our first retail location for profitability, growth, and an unmistakably “McGee” experience —As Told to Lila Allen

#4845. Home for the Holidays? 4 Survival Tips

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

Are you headed to a gathering of friends or family in the coming weeks? Here is a heads-up: A November 2026 survey of 538 people found that 8 out of 10 respondents anticipate that political differences will come up during holiday meals (The Conversation). Further, a meta-analysis controlling for various factors found that dinners involving folks with diverse political perspectives were shorter by 24 minutes than dinners with politically uniform ones (Frimer & Skitka, 2020). How exactly these meals ended 24 minutes earlier is unknown. Hopefully it wasn’t a food fight.

The bottom line? Many folks consider political talk at holiday meals anxiety-provoking, preferring to focus on bonding and nostalgia. And yet many still may feel it is important to “return fire” on political views they deem uninformed, misinformed, or downright harmful. Post-midterm elections, a meme circulating on social media suggests that you bring up politics at holiday dinners so you can save money on gift purchases this year. Alternatively, when first sitting down at the table, one could ask, “Are we sick of ‘winning’ yet?” If you love conflict during meals, saying these sorts of things is likely to spark it. If, however, you'd prefer to keep your gatherings calm, here are some tips to survive your get-togethers:

Set clear boundaries ahead of time. Decide beforehand the topics considered off-limits (for you or others to bring up). If folks insist that you engage with them on an off-limits subject, communicate your limits using a calm tone and then have a plan to step away should they persist. One option is to stand up and apologize for having to take a call, real or imaginary.

Forget about winning. When exchanges are conceptualized as sharing perspectives, it's easier to shift away from the idea that this is a high-stakes battle and that victory is a necessity. The goal could instead be civil conversation. Keep your eyes on that prize, no matter what Uncle Charlie says to provoke a reaction.

Adopt a curious stance. If an exchange on politics does happen, show strong interest in how the person came to the views they're expressing. If tension rises, acknowledge the difference briefly and steer back to food, shared memories, or helping out. The merits of pumpkin versus bourbon chocolate pecan pie can present a useful distraction.

Try listening. Intentional, active listening is an important skill, especially now in a world where people desperately seeking to be victors in verbal battles are simply preparing their next salvo rather than paying attention to what the other person is saying. Really listening sends a palpable message that the person we are speaking to matters.

In conclusion, people may not remember specific details of an exchange of political views later on, but they will likely recall how they felt while speaking with us, and this brings us back to the context of a holiday get-together. Warm memories are still possible if we permit our better angels to prevail. Please pass the bourbon chocolate pecan pie.

Frimer, J. A., & Skitka, L. J. (2020). Are politically diverse Thanksgiving dinners shorter than politically uniform ones? PloS one, 15(10), e0239988. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0239988

The Conversation. (November, 2026). Retrieved November 18, 2026, at: https://theconversation.com/thanksgiving-dinner-is-likely-to-be-served-…

#4844. I Tried Adding 10 Minutes of Daily Mobility to My Routine for Two Weeks. Here’s How My Body—And Mind—Changed

Plus, the expert-backed reason a few minutes of mobility can add up over time.

I’m in my early 30s, which means staying fit requires more of a conscious, consistent effort. The natural loss of lean muscle mass and skin elasticity that occurs at this stage of life makes me more mindful of my body and overall well-being. So, I’ve declared this my year of wellness. As part of it, I have been working on adding small bouts of movement that manageably fit into my daily life. Mobility work felt like one of the best ways to do that.

Mobility is an incredibly underrated training modality, yet it’s an essential part of healthy aging—especially for those like me who spend most of the day sitting at a desk. Mobility training focuses on controlled, active movement through a joint’s full range of motion, says Matthew Cifelli, PT, DPT, CSCS, of Attain Physical Therapy.

This style of movement helps you perform nearly every daily task, from climbing stairs and getting up from a seated position to walking with a full stride and turning your head while driving. But as you age or spend extended periods of time being sedentary, it’s common for muscles to tighten, joints to stiffen, and movement to become less efficient.

“Limited mobility forces the body to compensate with inefficient patterns, increasing the risk of pain, balance issues, and injury,” says Cifelli. Maintaining mobility, on the other hand, “supports independence, joint health, and the ability to move confidently through life.”

That’s why I recently decided to add just 10 minutes of mobility work to my daily routine for two weeks. Here’s exactly what I did—and how my body changed.

Mobility is “not just about ‘feeling loose,’” says Cifelli. “It's about teaching the body to use its flexibility in real movement.” It’s a mix of static stretching and flexibility work that focuses on muscle length. “Mobility training targets how well a joint moves and how well you control that motion, which requires coordinated muscle activation and joint stability.”

And just a few minutes a day of mobility work can help boost circulation, lubricate the joints, alleviate muscle tension, and improve confidence in daily movement. “Even short sessions, when done daily, create meaningful cumulative change,” he says.

My routine included a combination of exercises and hold times I learned from Portia Page, CPT, in addition to a couple of stretches my physical therapist recommended incorporating into my home regimen. I performed each exercise for one minute, one time through.

During the first week of my experiment, I eased into my 10-minute mobility routine. I was eager to see how it could help improve my “desk body,” a.k.a. tight hips, tense hamstrings, and lower back and neck tension.

I did the workout every morning around 8 a.m. before diving into the madness of the day. It was pretty seamless to add to my mornings, since I have a dedicated workout space in my home, though the routine doesn’t require much space or equipment. Plus, I’m someone who craves routine. Sticking to the same time each morning made this fitness habit sustainable.

From the get-go, it was clear my body was tense and in desperate need of some stretching and mobility work. My legs, back, and hips all felt stiff at the beginning of the workout. Certain exercises, like the standing forward fold, hip flexor stretch, and supine figure-four stretch were more challenging than the rest. For example, during the first week, I found it difficult to touch the floor when doing the forward fold, so I didn’t force it.

By the end of each session, my body was definitely a bit more relaxed, but I knew I needed to stick with mobility work for more than just a week or two in order to achieve meaningful, lasting results.

I was a dancer growing up, and my body was much more flexible then than it is now. While the Pilates classes I attend three to four times a week have definitely helped me stretch and strengthen my body, a dedicated mobility routine felt like exactly what the doctor ordered. I didn’t realize it would help me in my classes, too. By the end of week one, I felt I was able to move through a more seamless range of motion in certain Pilates exercises like the mermaid and the straight-back hinge on the short box.

Heading into week two, I found myself looking forward to my morning mobility session. It started to feel like more of a natural segue into my day, similar to brushing my teeth, taking my vitamins, or getting dressed. Once I wrapped up stretching and sat down at my desk, my body felt more limber and relaxed as I started work. However, after a couple hours of sitting, I felt much more tense again. The experiment taught me to be mindful of that: My body needs movement throughout the day—not just first thing in the morning.

I felt inspired by this healthy mobility habit and how great I feel afterward, so I wanted to keep the momentum going. During week two, I started building other healthy habits, like getting up to walk around my kitchen and living room every hour and going on a longer brisk walk at the end of the day. Both helped me stay limber throughout the day, rather than just in the morning. My hope is that, with all of these bouts of movement combined, sitting won’t undo all of the wonderful benefits I get from my stretching routine.

By the end of the second week, I was pleased that my body felt more accustomed to the dedicated mobility work than it had during week one. The more challenging stretches also became slightly easier, which made me feel like I was making genuine progress.

The routine became a no-brainer—a staple, if you will—in my morning routine: I’d wake up, brew a soothing latte, and get to work on my yoga mat. It also sparked the desire to get up and move more during the workday rather than remain hunched over my laptop for an extended period of time.

Because I experienced the tension-relieving benefits of this mobility work almost immediately after each session during week two, I’m now inspired to do it at both the start and end of my day. It’s a great way to ease any built-up stiffness after a long day at my desk before slipping into bed.

That said, one thing I’d love to continue working on is my posture. I didn’t experience any groundbreaking improvements during this two-week timeframe, but I’m hopeful that I’ll make progress down the line. I’m also curious to see whether being consistent with this mobility routine long-term will help my body—especially my hips and lower back—feel less stiff after sitting or lounging for longer periods.

Consistency is key. As with any workout, consistency is essential for success. But alas, it’s something I’ve struggled with over the years. Hectic work weeks filled with deadlines and appointments typically push my fitness to the back burner.

However, during this two-week test period, I was incredibly determined to carve out 10 minutes each day for my stretching regimen, and I’m so glad I did. Sticking with this fitness habit helped me feel better mentally and physically. My body started to feel more flexible and limber by the end of the two-week period—something I don’t think I would have experienced if I were inconsistent with my efforts.

According to Page, a mere 5 to 10 minutes a day of mobility work can make a noticeable difference over time if you’re consistent with the habit. She recommends thinking of stretching “not as a luxury but as basic maintenance for your body—like brushing your teeth.”

Kickstarting the day with fitness can promote other healthy habits. Starting the day with mobility work inspired me to follow other healthy habits throughout. After all, I was already off to a solid start and wanted to keep that momentum going strong.

Following each mobility session, I felt accomplished, energized, and ready to tackle the day. I found myself sticking with my regular Pilates workouts, making all-around healthier meal choices, snacking less, and adding brief “movement snacks” to my afternoons to break up the time spent sitting at my desk.

Mobility is a low-barrier starting point for movement. What I love best about this mobility workout? I don’t need to leave the comfort of my home or have access to fancy equipment. I’ve seamlessly incorporated these exercises into my self-care routine, and it just takes 10 minutes of my morning before I dive into work deadlines and commitments.

While there’s always room for improvement—and I’d like to add even more stretches to my routine—I felt incredibly accomplished overall with only a 10-minute routine. I’m hopeful that, by starting now and being consistent with mobility training, I can help prepare my body to tackle everyday tasks with ease. This training can also help me stay mobile, confident, and independent in my adventurous lifestyle for the long term.

Alexa is a content strategist, editor, and writer based in Greenwich, Connecticut, who has more than 12 years of experience writing for travel, lifestyle, and fitness publications. Alexa’s work has appeared in Business Insider, Parade, Men's Journal, Apartment Therapy, Men’s Fitness, Allrecipes, Family Handyman, Eat This, Not That!, Body Network, Everyday Health, SheBuysTravel, Tasting Table, Elite Daily, and more. When she’s not writing, you’ll likely find her at Pilates, hiking, designing her next tablescape, or jetting off on a getaway.

#4842. In Jordyn Woods-Towns’s NYC Home, Every Day is Knicksmas: “The Whole House Is Knicks-ed Out Already!”

The most wonderful time of the year holds a special place in Jordyn Woods-Towns’s heart—and no, we’re not talking about the start of basketball season. The fashion designer got engaged to Knicks phenom Karl-Anthony Towns on Christmas Eve 2025, and after a whirlwind 2026 including an NBA championship win for the New York NBA team (possibly courtesy of her viral accessory-turned-amulet) and a clifftop wedding replete with stunning details, the couple can’t wait to create festive memories as husband and wife.

“This is my first married Christmas,” Woods-Town tells AD. “I’ve only been married three months, but it’s our first holiday season, so I definitely need to try to figure out what our new traditions are.”

The newlywed reveals that she created an entire PowerPoint presentation to prep attendees for her bachelorette party, so you’d best believe she appreciates a little organization when it comes to getting in the spirit for big days. Planner that she is, Woods-Towns linked up with design marketplace Minted for her first family Christmas card and a curated suite of picks to welcome one particularly merry and bright yuletide season of life. Below, AD gets her take on holiday colors, basketball-themed decor, and more.

In anticipation of the holiday season, Woods-Towns teamed up with Minted to curate a selection of festive stationery and decor.

Architectural Digest: Have you always been a big holiday person?

Jordyn Woods-Towns: Every single season, I decorate. On Valentine’s Day I have the girls over to do a charcuterie board with salami roses and chocolate covered strawberries. Karl and I went crazy for Halloween; we turned the entire front yard into a whole different space with a graveyard and a 20-foot-tall skeleton. On Christmas, I love a theme.

For a couple years I went with a Candy Cane Lane vibe and now I’m in my chic New York era. I love a Ralph Lauren Christmas. I love the natural linen and natural materials. I’ve been really into natural florals, textural things. I love feathers, incorporating some ostrich feathers throughout—I do a lot of that with my brand, and I feel like feathers are really having a moment right now.

In New York it’s been hard because I don’t drive and I don’t have my car. I can’t just run down to HomeGoods, grab something, and come back!

What’s your decor looking like this year?

I’ve been really into all one shade. There were a lot of greens in our wedding and green is my color of the season.

Woods-Towns is leaning toward florals and green for holiday decorating this year.

The tree’s already green. It could be kind of cool, full green-on-green. Now I’m the Grinch. [laughs]

With your Christmas Eve engagement last year, the holiday is a sweet part of your love story. What sorts of traditions are you looking forward to starting with Karl?

I started with the holiday card with Minted. This is our first holiday card as a family. Obviously after you have kids, it kind of changes, but right now we’re at a time where life is just… he has a [Christmas Day] game and so we’re like, “Okay, we’re living the young, fast life.” But as time goes on, as our marriage goes on, we’re going to build different traditions. We love to be with our family and I always cook every holiday, so I’ll definitely be cooking after the game.

Is there a signature dish you like to serve?

Karl’s a picky eater. He loves chicken, so some version of chicken. He’s never had beef or pork or anything in his whole entire life. It’s just us, so some type of chicken and sides. Pretty simple.

I wanted to use a photo from our wedding that really felt like us, something that not everyone has seen, to tie in our whole year. It was a green marbled border design with gold foil border by Jenna Holcomb. There are those shades of green, since there’s a lot of green incorporated into our wedding. Olive is very timeless, and it felt chic and like us, like something that people could keep. I don’t want to say everyone’s going to want to put a photo of us in their house, but I know our family [will].

The Towns family’s holiday card. The design is “Marbled” by Jenna Holcomb.

Are you hosting bigger parties this season or just keeping it more intimate with the celebrations?

No huge parties, just because I don’t have the capacity to do that right now, but definitely getting the family together. We don’t have a huge family, so it should be pretty intimate, hopefully doing something with the team getting together. I think one of the girls was talking about doing a holiday party—even though I love to be the host, I don’t mind just showing up.

I would say it’s all in the details. I think through everything. But overall, it’s about the vibe that you’re bringing, the energy, and what you’re putting out. People remember the music, the food, and how they felt.

It’s been a busy 2026 for Woods-Towns between then-fiancé Karl-Anthony Towns’s successful championship run with the New York Knicks and her August wedding, but she’s keeping her energy high heading into holiday party season. “I feel like there’s an event every other day. But it’s not going to be like this forever. I had to change my mindset from, ‘Wow, I’m so tired,’ to, ‘Wow, I’m so lucky to be able to do this.’”

Are you planning on sprinkling any Knicks Easter eggs throughout your home decor or in your gifting this year?

There’s so many Knicks things in my house that it’s hard to escape. It’s already everywhere, the whole house is Knicks-ed out already! But I don’t mind Knicks-themed gifting—people love the Knicks.

Karl’s very hard to gift for, and his birthday’s actually right before the holidays. So it’s hard to figure out two really good gifts in a short amount of time. Gift giving is one of my love languages, and I love getting people things that they really can utilize in their everyday life. I need to think about that.

How else do you get in the holiday spirit at home?

I already bought Christmas pajamas and I already watched The Grinch twice with my niece and nephew two days ago. So I’m ready!

#4840. James Gray on Paper Tiger, Adam Driver, and Why Great Leading Men Need Danger and Vulnerability

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

The filmmaker talks ambition, masculinity, and why he’s always trying to mine his own life for the truth.

ONCE YOU’VE GONE to outer space with Brad Pitt and almost gotten eaten in the Amazon, where else is there to head but home? That’s the question filmmaker James Gray asked himself after wrapping the World War I-era adventure epic The Lost City of Z and the celestial adventure Ad Astra. His answer: “I guess the conscious desire was to go back to what I know.”

That resulted, first, in 2022’s Armageddon Time, a largely autobiographical story of a young Gray growing up in Queens with his imperfect parents (Anne Hathaway and Jeremy Strong) and loving grandfather (Anthony Hopkins). His latest film, Paper Tiger, was originally conceived as a sequel to that one, but eventually settled into a separate mostly autobiographical and intimate tale of the director’s youth.

The new film once again features characters explicitly based on his parents, this time with the bespectacled father, Irwin, played by Miles Teller and the expressive mother, Hester, played by Scarlett Johansson. Naive Irwin gets drawn into a sketchy business plan by his brash brother Gary, a former cop and ambitious entrepreneur played by Adam Driver—and things only go south when Irwin proudly decides to show his new venture off to his sons and sees something he should not have.

Paper Tiger also marks a return to Gray’s roots as a teller of crime stories that will stop you in your tracks. (Longtime fans will remember he made his directorial debut with the Tim Roth-led hitman thriller Little Odessa in 1994.) But what could be just another crime drama in the hands of a lesser filmmaker becomes a grounded human story about the downside of ambition with Gray. His films are arresting because they feel like they could happen to you, too.

This new film, then, allowed the 57-year-old director to continue doing what he’s done his whole career: tell stories that, while lightly fictionalized, are still, at their core, true—regardless of genre. “I don’t see the movies as ‘crime dramas,’ even though clearly that’s what they are, because that’s part of the fabric of my young life growing up,” he says. “In my father’s case, and in my family’s case, it’s in our DNA. And so, for me, what is simply a memory of some sort, becomes quantifiable as a crime drama. Really, what you’re seeing is me trying to be very sincere with you about my own experience.”

It’s a story that’s been deep within him for a long time—and one he’s glad to have finally purged. “Now that I’ve gotten out of my system a little, I’m ready to expand the palette again,” he says.

As Paper Tiger expands to a nationwide release in theaters, Gray spoke with Men’s Health about finding great leading men, mining his life for stories, and the key to making everything personal.

Plus—read Gray’s take on his former Lost City of Z star Robert Pattinson as James Bond, from just a couple of days before the casting became official.

MEN’S HEALTH: You’ve worked with stars like Brad Pitt, Joaquin Phoenix, and Charlie Hunnam, and now Paper Tiger adds Adam Driver and Miles Teller to that list. So, what makes a great leading man?

JAMES GRAY: To be completely candid, some aspect of what you’re asking is unknowable until you see it on screen. It’s funny, I was reading about the casting of Peter O’Toole in Lawrence of Arabia. He had never done anything on screen, and all of a sudden they put him in the movie, and there’s magic. There are other people who you try to put in movies over and over again, and it never really clicks, for whatever reason. There’s an intangible quality to a great actor that we almost never can put our finger on.

That said, I’m looking for an ability to convey two things at once: danger and vulnerability. A sensitivity. Often, what you find is it comes from intelligence. I’ve never worked with a great dumb actor. It does not exist. If the actor is marvelous—and I’ve been lucky enough to work with almost exclusively great actors—they are all brilliant in an emotional way. Does it mean they can quote Proust? No, but that doesn’t matter. They have an emotional awareness, and they can read a room, and they have a shrewdness. All of this stuff goes into the work, because if you have a close-up of an actor, you can immediately see what they’re thinking, if they are thinking. I’m looking for both danger and vulnerability, in kind of equal measure. And you see it over and over in great performances. In fact, I can only think of one performance in all of cinema history, really only one, that is both great and has no danger in it, and that would be what Jeff Bridges does in The Big Lebowski. It has no danger at all, but it’s still a great performance. I’m not exactly sure how he pulled it off—it’s a real achievement. Maybe because he’s so sensitive and lovable in it that you fall for him, you know? But almost always, you have to have that aspect.

MH: When you’re casting for movies like Paper Tiger and Armageddon Time, which are ostensibly based on your own life, do you feel more of a pressure to make sure you get it right, as opposed to a story you’re perhaps a layer removed from, like The Lost City of Z?

JG: It’s funny, I’m not sure how much difference there is. I know Lost City of Z is about a guy in Edwardian England going into Amazonia, but when I was conceiving of that movie, I never tried to distance myself from Percy Fawcett at all. I tried to, in fact, invest myself in him. He was a dreamer, someone who felt slighted by the system, and he wanted to prove himself over and over again. He didn’t have medals. He wanted to be celebrated, and he finally gets celebrated, and he needs more. All of that is in us.

So, your question is a very good one, but in all truth, I’m trying—and maybe you don’t succeed, of course—in all cases to put myself into the work. That’s what I would say is making something personal. That’s very different from making something autobiographical. Autobiographical adheres to the facts of your life, and it is true—these last two pictures have been quite autobiographical. But that’s just so that hopefully I have an easier time in getting at what it is that I’m thinking about. They’re different modes, but you’re still trying to do the same thing, which is to get at your interiority.

MH: Miles Teller plays a character based on your father. I’ve never seen him do anything like what he does in Paper Tiger. What sold you on him?

JG: I had seen a bunch of his work, and I’d also spoken to my esteemed assistant director, a wonderful, beautiful man named Doug Torres, who’d worked on a movie with Miles Teller. I knew about him through him, and also the people that had worked with him. I had seen a film called Bleed for This, where he plays Vinny Pazienza, and his performance has what we were just talking about. He’s a boxer, he has a toughness, but it’s a very vulnerable performance. I didn’t want to lean into the nebbish, schlub aspect to the character at all. I wanted the character to have a certain fortitude, because then the vulnerability can really come through. In other words, if you’re just casting a movie and the guy is a nerd or whatever, and you’re watching a nerd be nerdy, it’s not that interesting. What I found was that Miles has an alpha quality, but to see a tenderness inside of that was the thing that really interested me. And I saw it in that film.

MH: Adam Driver is a sensational actor too. What was the appeal and experience of working with Adam?

JG: Adam has a very powerful onscreen dark quality, but he’s also open. He does completely different things from take to take. He’s always trying to find something new, something inventive. And he has tremendous craft. You can tell he’s really studied, and so you have both the craft and also he’s not in a rut. It’s just small things sometimes that you fall in love with. You’ve seen the film—he comes into the house, he brings Peter Luger’s, and he grabs the lamp, you know? A piece of set dressing. And he holds it under his face, and he says, “Tonight, Luger’s is coming to us.” So, all of a sudden, he’s like a showman. It’s these little touches, where he understands character. And again, I know I’m repeating myself—this comes from intelligence. He’s incredibly intelligent. He sees bullshit a mile away. That is a very good thing for an actor. He is a truth-teller. Great actors are truth machines. They will not let you lie in a scene. They are always open to the moment.

MH: That character is fascinating to me, because in other movies like this, he might turn into a villain. But your story plays with such shades of gray, and it really stands out.

JG: The idea was to set up a scenario where you see the guy and your immediate impression might be “Oh, he’s a cop, he’s bringing food over. He must be a jerk, or he’s trying to scheme, or something.” But in fact it turns out the exact opposite; he had nothing but very pure intentions, and winds up sacrificing himself. That was very much part of taking the audience’s expectations and subverting them. Now, when you do something like that, you’re going to have, hopefully, a small percentage of the audience, whining and complaining, telling you What are you doing there? How could he be naive? But you’re also going to have a large percentage of the audience that’s going to embrace the fact that it’s not a cliché. I was leaning into the sense Adam has as an actor, saying, “Yes, but we’re going to trick you.” And in the end, he’s going to have a generosity and a nobility to his character.

MH: Adam’s character is really brash and confident—it seems like he’s used to getting what he wants and isn’t afraid to kick some ass. Miles’s character, on the other hand, is a lot more reserved and sometimes naive. How did you go about designing the story around these two guys who each carry a very different brand of masculinity and see the world in different ways?

JG: It’s interesting you bring that up, because the operating principle of the movie… I was up very late one night, and I was watching—as one would—C-SPAN, I guess to try to put myself to sleep. And sometimes they televise the speeches that CEOs give at Davos, or that kind of thing. And I saw the CEO of a large corporation, and he was giving a speech, and he said “95% of people don’t know there’s a game.” He said, “Of the remaining 5%, 4% know there’s a game and don’t know how to play it, and then the top 1% know how to play it, and will win.”

I think his percentages are off—I think there are a lot more people who know there’s a game but don’t know how to play it, and that’s why we have a lot of anger in the world. But I thought of the story this way. You have Gary, a character who knows there’s a game, and knows how to play it, but he won’t make the ethical and moral compromises to win. You’ve got Irwin, who knows there’s a game, but has no idea how to play it. He’s smart—he’s an engineer. But he’s not shrewd. It’s a very different intelligence. And then you’ve got Scarlett, who probably knows there’s a game and maybe even knows how to play it, but fate has a different plan for her. So, the movie was organized along these principles. That this idea that our society always rewards the smartest and best, that it’s a meritocracy, is not really true. It rewards a certain kind of smarts, along with a certain kind of willingness to compromise. I saw Adam and Miles in this framework.

MH: Do you often find the germ of an idea in mundane places like watching C-SPAN in the middle of the night?

JG: One of the horrible things about creativity, and it’s also one of the truths, is that it is a very mercurial, impatient, sometimes too patient, thing, and sometimes ideas come to you in the most random of ways. The biggest obligation you have to your imagination is your willingness to make the random idea connect. In other words, the essence of creativity is your ability to make connections. So, sometimes, you get inspiration from totally bizarre sources that you’d never imagine. It’s up to your imagination to be open to the randomness of these connections, and to try and pull from them the source of your idea. It can sometimes be totally different, like, you’re in nature, you get an idea, or you hear someone, a homeless man, say something—that’s an idea. It can come from anywhere. And then we have the idea, of course, of myth, to give it some kind of structure. But the random idea is of tremendous value. It can come from C-SPAN, or it can come from a baby crying. It’s all part of the soup.

MH: With this movie, as you have so often throughout your career, you’re mining from your own life. I’m sure many of these memories are painful, so how do you protect yourself emotionally and mentally to avoid falling into a dark and difficult place?

JG: It’s an excellent question, and the answer is that you kind of can’t. I wish I could give you a glib response—the way that I protect myself is X—but what I owe you, really, is something that is honest, that is sincere. And I don’t owe you the idea that I should make myself look good, and that you should like me. I owe you my own version of the truth. So, if I’m working, it’s not fun all the time. Sometimes, you have to do things that are uncomfortable, that are unflinching, that are honest. And it’s not always pleasant. We recreated a fight between my parents, when my mother hit my father. Scarlett and Miles created it almost exactly as I recall it. This is my job. That’s why I do it. I do it to give it to you. And through that, you find the air of compassion and sympathy for a collective experience.

In other words, you’re not presenting a fantasy that has no relationship to honest emotion. And, by the way, when I say ‘fantasy,’ I don’t mean Star Wars can’t do it. Star Wars can do that. When he says, “No, Luke, I am your father,” that is actually connecting to something real, in the guise of a fantasy. When I say ‘fantasy,’ what I really mean is the filmmaker is trying to get you to like him or her or them, and that’s not my job. Sometimes you go to these unpleasant places, and it’s my job to cope.

MH: You’ve mentioned expanding your palette now that you’ve gotten these stories out of your system—do you have anything specific in mind? Is there anything you haven’t done yet that you want to try to tackle?

JG: I would love to do a Western. I would love to do a horror movie. I can’t believe I’m going to say this—I would love to do a musical. I don’t know what kind of shape the musical would take, but all of these genres are different forms of expression of the same ideas. I find the Westerns of John Ford unbelievably powerful to this day, because they’re always expressing something that’s inside Ford. Especially the films he made after World War II, which have such a thread of loss in them. And they’re very powerful to this day. You see John Wayne struggling with moral and ethical catastrophes in The Searchers, and you see a kind of post-war reckoning with what was a catastrophe of moral proportions in World War II, and you see it in John Wayne. You see the person of Ford coming out in that way, and using it in that canvas, the American West. That’s beautiful, and a way into the dark side of our personalities. Really, it becomes about me trying to find a story that will accommodate that, and that’s the difficult thing.

#4838. 9 Best Small Sectional Sofas That Are Truly Stylish (2026)

A sprawling living room might be the dream, but having a small space doesn’t preclude you from being able to stretch out on the couch. Sectionals specifically designed for smaller rooms prove that cozy movie nights and afternoon naps aren’t reserved exclusively for those with a massive floor plan. In fact, choosing a sectional with the right proportions stands to make a smaller room feel larger. There’s no reason to settle for a hodgepodge of chairs and ottomans when a thoughtfully selected sectional can transform every seat into the best seat in the house.

Being mindful of a space’s dimensions is always important when shopping for furniture, but especially so with a small room, where every inch may matter. Still, a variety of clever configurations—including L-shaped sectionals designed to nestle into corners, modular designs that are easily rearranged, and sofas with reversible chaises that give you more flexibility—cater to seemingly every layout. Add in performance fabrics, washable slipcovers, and supportive cushions, and you’ve got a recipe for some seriously comfortable yet compact lounging. Ahead, we’re sharing our favorite sectionals for small spaces that ensure every square foot counts.

The best-selling Abisko sectional from Article is made even more beautiful by colorful, performance velvet upholstery. Suitable for those with little ones and pets running around, the fabric is non-absorptive, meaning spills and crumbs won’t stay embedded in its weave. Two orientations—chaise and L-shaped—allow you to Tetris its silhouette into your space as you see fit.

Instead of opting for a giant L-shaped sectional that will take up the entire room, aim for something with a smaller footprint. Available in performance fabric and three leg finishes, this sectional couch is ideal for a tiny living space and a major upgrade from a smaller loveseat thanks to the chaise addition. While not an official fold-out sleeper sofa, the back cushions flop back to give you enough space should you be inclined to nap. Contributor David Kaufman, who tested it out for us, calls it “a great starter sofa for a first home or apartment that you won’t have to send to a landfill when you’re ready to move.”

Similar to the Thuma sectional contributor Evan Russum told us “feels solid and durable,” the Essential Sofa follows the brand’s signature simple-but-considered aesthetic with a minimalist silhouette,rounded cushions, and a grounded wooden base. Raised armrests add sculptural presence without overwhelming a small living room, while the detachable ottoman lets you switch between a left- or right-facing chaise—so everyone can have a turn on their favorite side of the sofa.

Not your average grey couch, AllModern’s Jossa sectional is minimalist in looks but generous on comfort, thanks to its dense foam padding that offers plenty of support without feeling stiff. Easy to de-assemble, the modular design allows the sofa to evolve with your seating needs. Craving two separate lounge chairs? Done. Prefer a love seat? Just slide the two larger seats side-by-side. Today’s layout doesn’t have to be tomorrow’s.

The slim arms and low profile on this this reversible three-piece sectional make the Unwind especially suitable for a limited living area as it doesn’t monopolize the space. Five neutral color variations all come in a linen blend, but olive’s grounding tones are speaking most to us. This sectional, like many of the others on this list, can be configured to be left-facing or right-facing depending on your living room setup, and we particularly like that in case you tend to switch up your design layout (we certainly do).

At just 62 inches wide, Sabai’s Essential Loveseat Sectional demonstrates how even the smallest living rooms can accommodate a proper chaise lounge. The compact design features clean lines, a generously sized chaise, and supportive foam cushions, offering the ideal spot to stretch out after a long day. Adding to the sectional’s appeal is its focus on sustainability. It combines a frame made from wood certified by the Forest Stewardship Council (FSC)—a third-party verification that ensures ethical wood sourcing—with upholstery fashioned from recycled natural materials. It’s also easy to clean and maintain, largely thanks to its washable slipcovers, sold separately—a welcome feature for anyone whose couch often doubles as a dining chair for meals eaten over the coffee table. Suffice it to say, this sectional is particularly well-suited to apartment living.

CB2’s Deseo sectional brings a little drama to small-space living, courtesy of rich, praline-brown performance velvet, broad arms, and a low-slung silhouette that practically begs you to sink in and stay awhile. The three-piece configuration, matching ottoman, and option for an extra-deep seat only extend the lounging possibilities and allow you to take advantage of every inch of your space. If brown doesn’t fit your space’s palette, worry not; the Deseo comes in plenty of other glamorous colors, including seven other performance velvet upholstery options.

Serious lounging is the goal for Sundays’ Movie Night sectional, with oversized cushions, deep seats, and a relaxed silhouette that makes it difficult to resist the urge to spend the afternoon totally horizontal. The cream linen upholstery adds to its laid-back feel, while the movable ottoman lets you stretch out or create a more open seating arrangement when company comes over. The company’s own LiveLife performance fabric is stain-resistant, moisture-repellent, and washable, with removable slipcovers that make living with a light-colored sofa significantly less intimidating.

Interior Define takes customization very seriously, and the Sloan sectional showcases how having such options can pay off in a small living room. Choose your preferred upholstery, cushion fill, seat depth, and leg style, then fine-tune the dimensions to suit your floor plan. The reversible chaise adds another layer of flexibility, allowing you to change its orientation, in case you rearrange your furniture or move to a new place with a different layout.

Contributor Malia Griggs tested the Sloan in her own 196-square-foot living room, where she found that its supportive cushions, tailored silhouette, and carefully selected dimensions worked beautifully alongside a narrow entryway. “If you enjoy tailoring your décor to your taste, are willing to pay a bit more for quality, and have the patience for a made-to-order process, this is a wonderful sectional—especially for a smaller space,” she added.

What Features Should I Look for in a Sectional for Small Living Rooms?

Modular furniture—any sectional that comes in several parts so you can adjust your sofa to suit the configurations—is built with flexibility in mind, making it the ideal contender for a small living space. We have tested and loved Castlery modular sofas, but a search for modular sectional should give you plenty of other options. A room tight on space can benefit from couches with storage, like those from Albany Park. Now you’ll be able to minimize the clutter and extra blankets by stowing them underneath your seat.

How Do I Arrange a Sectional in a Small Space?

Don’t fall for the tiniest sectional you can find, but rather invest in something well-made—it plays a big part in your living room, after all. While it may seem counterintuitive, Nashville interior designer Amanda Khouri says, “Filling a small room with small furniture can make it feel…well, smaller.”

Designer Alicia Murphy used a sectional in the living room of a teensy trailer she converted into a plush family getaway in Montauk, New York, for this very reason: “If you use a corner sectional rather than a sofa and chair, you most likely will add seating for two or three more people,” Murphy explains, noting that the alternative prevents you from having about 36 inches of dead space in the corner.”

Another way to make it work? Set an L-shaped sectional across from two club chairs to create a conversation zone, advises interior designer Suzanne Dawson.

What Do I Look for in a High-Quality Sectional?

When you’re working with a small space, quality counts. It’s much harder to get away with a mid-century modern knock-off when it’s one of four furniture pieces packed into the room. When shopping for a sectional, evaluate the materials and care instructions. Avoid anything with plywood, and polyester when you can. Seek out solid wood construction, such as walnut, oak, or teak; and premium fabrics, like linen, leather, or chenille. You’ll also want to keep the warranty and return policy in mind, in case you want to send back a piece that doesn’t work for you.
