#4817. A Fantastical Perch Above Toulon’s Old Port, Where Mermaids Meet Mediterranean Light

Though perhaps not well known outside France, Vincent Darré is one of Paris’s most familiar figures—always on the scene, day and night. The impish designer rarely just enters a room; he bounces in, impeccably dressed, with an infectious laugh and beautiful manners. At home in the worlds of fashion, society, art, and design, he is welcome at every table, always ready with a clever remark, a kind word, and no shortage of creative energy.

From his early days in fashion, which included stints at Moschino and Ungaro and a close, yearslong collaboration with none other than Karl Lagerfeld, Darré has followed a singular path, turning his creative energies to furniture and interiors with the opening of his own studio, Maison Darré, in 2008. A pair of recently completed Paris hotels—L’Aventure, at the foot of the Arc de Triomphe, and Hôtel Le Magnifique, in the heart of Montparnasse—are propelling him onto the design scene in a bigger way than ever. His work has long encompassed scenography and ephemeral installations, among them crowd-pleasing turns at AD Intérieurs, the erstwhile annual showcase hosted by AD France.

In the formal salon, a pair of carved wood armchairs with inlaid stone backs have seat cushions of a Dedar fabric. Darré-designed objects include his Calder table, Minos rug, and Lyre mirror. He also created the trompe-l’oeil pilasters topped with 18th-century gilded wooden capitals. Late-19th-century French lantern; 1940s Italian ceramic dolphin table.

In the guest bedroom, Darré sits on an 18th-century gilded wood bench upholstered in velvet by Métaphores. A Darré-painted mural frames the 18th century Italian headboard upholstered in Tony Duquette’s Xanadu fabric for Jim Thompson. The bedcover and cushions are from Darré’s collection for Monoprix.

Darré was born in Paris, in the 14th, and went to school there as a boy. When his parents separated in the 1970s, his father—a sociologist—moved to the Luberon, and Vincent went with him; not long after, his mother, unwilling to live far from her son, also moved south, to Montpellier. “This allowed me to be Parisian, but also one who knew other places,” he says. It’s a telling detail: the South of France has informed his eye ever since, with its particular sense of light, water, and ease. Though he first went to school for fashion, his real love was drawing, as it had been since childhood. “Sometimes people are surprised,” he notes, “that a finished work of mine is almost always exactly like I had drawn it.”

After a series of Paris apartments over the years, Darré has recently acquired a getaway in Toulon, the Mediterranean port city. The attraction was immediate. He had been invited to preside over the jury of Design Parade, the summer design festival held in Toulon and Hyères, and the city seized him the moment he arrived. “Once I got to the airport, in 2017, I immediately felt I was home. Chez moi! I had never experienced that feeling before.” He kept an eye on the listings and, after a few false starts, found exactly what he wanted.

In the entrance, Darré’s Vase Soleil stands atop a 1940s Venetian console table against a wall decorated with trompe l’oeil caryatids.

A 19th-century rattan sofa upholstered in Jean Lurçat’s Sirenes fabric by Pierre Frey.

Overlooking the Toulon harbor, the primary bedroom’s office area features several Darré designs including his Orphée sconce, Singez-moi table lamp, the carved and lacquered wood desk, a Vertebré chair cushioned in a fabric by Pierre Le-Tan, and a Column stool.

Lion head mascarons flank the doorway into the primary bedroom. 1970s plaster Buddha lamps with Darré-painted shades stand atop 17th-century French consoles. A 1960s plaster seahorse is displayed in the fireplace.

The apartment occupies the top floor of a little three-story house overlooking the fishing port—a compact 860 square feet with stunning views of the sea. It was already lovely when he moved in, all white, with nothing architectural to be done: the perfect backdrop for Darré and his pencils and paints. He brought many of his favorite things—collections, objects, and furniture gathered over the years, added to since at the Drouot auction house and the little brocantes he loves to haunt. Furnishing was, he says, a gradual process, bringing in pieces little by little and slowly making the space his own over time.

Darré’s Crocodile bench stands in the primary bedroom. Two-Faced lamps with hand-painted shades atop Pas Gigogne tables flank the bed, and his Poisson bookcase is at left. The plaster chandelier is by Mathieu Challières, and the plaster unicorns are from a set designed by Jean Cocteau.

A metal figure given to Darré by Ines de la Fressange stands next to his Singez-moi lamp on the office area desk.

Darré’s Tabou shelf in the primary bedroom

Darré on his Column stool with a 19th-century gilt-wood mirror from a Paris flea market

Darré speaks often of his love for Toulon, and of Jean Cocteau, who adored this coast and painted frescoes nearby. “I like the sweetness of life here,” he says. “Nothing has really changed since the 1950s. It’s the Provence of another era.” Every little square has its fountain; everyone is kind. It’s a military port, but its douceur de vie is what holds him.

The apartment represents Vincent Darré to a T: not an unadorned surface in sight, a home full of memories, tributes, and joy. “This has been one of my dreams, to have a house on the water,” he says. “My place in Paris is exactly the same, though not on the water. But both are little suspended palaces. I create my own follies.” From the painted columns flanking the windows—among his very first purchases, which have followed him from home to home—to the mermaids and sea creatures and the tented bed, everything belongs to the fantastical world of Darré. As one of his teachers observed early on, you could recognize his hand from the very start.

A close-up of Darré’s ceramic Two-Faced lamp

The dining area features a red lacquer table and chairs with Darré’s Dolphin lamp in the corner.

That world is entirely his own. He draws on a lineage of great fantasists—Charles de Beistegui, Henri Samuel, Jean Cocteau, Christian Bérard, Tony Duquette—yet the result, for all its jumble, is rigorously coherent. His flourish is always present. As the actress Isabelle Adjani once told him, to enter one of his interiors is to step into one of his drawings. Which is exactly what he wants.

For all the bounce in his step, Darré is no one’s fool. He knows we live in difficult times, and likes the idea of adding a flourish of fantasy to reality. “I have my little world—a dream universe, but one you can live in.” He loves to dance, and even took tap-dancing lessons as a teenager, all the better to channel Fred Astaire or Gene Kelly. “Life is a film, and we are the actors,” he says. “That’s why I always dress the way I do.” Lights, camera, action—Darré is always ready.

#4815. Menopause Was a Hushed Conversation—Until Gen X Changed Everything

An entire generation of younger women is being educated in the process.

Sharon Cancio, 28, didn’t grow up knowing much about menopause. She didn’t learn anything about it in school, nor from the women in her family. But when she was a teenager, she started noticing her mother’s mood shifting. Around her mid-to-late 40s, “she became much snappier, more easily irritated, and sometimes just seemed angry in a way that felt completely different from the mom I remembered growing up,” she recalls. “I genuinely thought life had simply worn her down.”

Cancio didn’t start connecting the dots until she came off birth control at 25 and noticed how dramatically her own mood changed around her cycle. Once she realized her mother had entered perimenopause, she went down an internet rabbit hole to learn about it. Women were discussing—in detail—what was happening to their bodies on TikTok and Reddit. Some women were going through menopause early, others were seeking answers for their symptoms.

These discussions are a far cry from what conversations around menopause used to look like: nonexistent. In the past, there wasn’t much education—or even real discussion—on what happens to the female body after 40, forcing women to hustle through hot flashes and mood swings behind closed doors.

But within the last few years, there’s been a shift: Gen X women are the first to go through this hormonal transition in the age of social media—and they’re not afraid to talk about their experiences, says Gillan Goddard, MD, an endocrinologist and an adjunct assistant professor of medicine at the NYU Langone Hospital. They’re educating an entire generation of younger women in the process. Posts about brain fog, inconsistent sleep patterns, and unfamiliar-feeling bodies have become the first real health literacy that this generation’s daughters, Gen Zers, have gotten about their own hormonal futures. These small conversations have big implications when it comes to learning more about their future health.

The lack of menopause education starts in classrooms: Almost all U.S. states require teenagers to learn about puberty, reproductive health, and sexual disease prevention through sex education classes. But the content and depth of those classes may not favor women’s health: A 2024 study in the Journal of School Health looked at the state of menstrual health education in U.S. K-12 public schools. Researchers analyzed the education standards from each state’s Department of Education site, searching terms like “menstruation,” “menopause,” “period,” “reproduction,” and “puberty.” It found that menstrual health education—especially menopause—is profoundly rare.

There’s also a lack of menopause education in medical schools. Only 31.3 percent of U.S. ob-gyn residency programs include a menopause curriculum, according to a 2023 study in Menopause. The result resembles a serious disconnect: The transition affects nearly half of the population, but the majority of the doctors tasked with treating menopause have received almost no training on how to do it.

Menopause just isn’t prioritized during residency training. Instead, the “focus during training was placed on surgical skills and labor and delivery responsibilities, both considered more urgent and time-consuming,” says Alyssa Dweck, MD, chief medical officer of Bonafide Health and a Menopause Society Certified Practitioner located in New York City. Ob-gyns can earn certifications in (peri)menopause, from organizations including the Menopause Society and Integrative Women’s Health Institute—but they’re not required. Clinicians should have more comprehensive training in medical school and beyond, says Dr. Dweck. But there should also be more funding and resources for women’s health research for treatment options.

When doctors aren’t familiar with menopause, “mood changes, cognitive changes, and body aches are often misunderstood or ignored,” says Dr. Goddard. This can lead to misdiagnoses, and to women not receiving proper treatment for symptoms caused by menopause. This is pretty common: A 2025 survey conducted by health care company Biote of over 1,000 women ages 30 to 60 in the U.S. found that 39 percent of women have been misdiagnosed and prescribed medication by a provider for conditions like depression.

TikTok and Instagram have filled the menopause education void in the U.S. Conversations about life in menopause have spread awareness about what the condition is actually like, crushing stigmas. This visibility is not only helping younger viewers learn what they can expect later in life—it’s also helping mothers start more health-forward conversations with their daughters.

Milan Parker, 25, has always had open conversations about health with her mom. “She’s always been really honest with me about what she’s going through, even the more personal parts that people sometimes consider taboo,” she says. But social media increased this dynamic tenfold: Parker’s mother underwent a hysterectomy due to fibroids at 48, which made her enter early menopause. Following the surgery, her mother joined a menopause support group on Facebook. “Seeing that there were women all across the country going through similar things made her more open to talking to me about it,” Parker says.

For instance, Parker’s mom finally explained how debilitating her hot flashes really were. (She’d stopped going on trips with her because she was embarrassed about looking sweaty.) “There were times when I thought maybe my mom just didn’t want to go out with me,” she says. “I’m really grateful that she made it something we could actually talk about instead of something that had to stay a secret.”

For daughters, it can be hard to watch their mothers struggle in menopause and not know how to help, but the experience can also help them grow closer. “The emotional experience can be a mix of empathy, grief, anxiety, and closeness,” says Ashley Peña, LCSW, a clinical social worker and the vice president of outpatient operations at A Mission for Michael.

Even though Cancio’s mom didn’t tell her when she was going through menopause, the experience helped her gain compassion for her mother and better understand her own body. “As a teenager, I honestly thought she was just becoming grumpy or ‘getting old,’ which I feel terrible admitting now,” she says. “As an adult woman, I have so much more empathy.”

Having a raw look at what menopause is actually like—whether through a screen or a conversation with their mother—shapes how younger women view aging and how to prepare themselves for what’s ahead. Hearing that they may one day inevitably experience sleepless nights, sudden anger, brain fog, and the loss of identity can be scary, to say the least. But “open conversation about menopause helps women hear the full scope of menopause experiences and how women dealt effectively with their symptoms,” Dr. Goddard says. It can make the condition sound less scary to younger women.

In fact, growing conversations around menopause can actually inspire younger women to learn about it earlier. “I am seeing patients of all ages, Gen Z included, who have become more inquisitive and engaged in their health overall,” Dr. Dweck says. Some of her young patients have told her they’ve already started talking to their older relatives about menopause and hormone health. They’re also more open about discussing fertility and egg freezing.

Even though menopause is now common dinner table conversation, the root of the (non-communication) issue still needs to be fixed. “The only way we normalize talking about women’s health is by talking about it,” Cancio says. “Ask questions, stay curious, and don’t be afraid to learn from women who have already been through it.”

Mothers going through (peri)menopause can have a series of casual conversations about it with their kids. (The earlier, the better.) They can keep the conversation casual and tailored to the child’s developmental age. For instance, moms with children under the age of 13 can briefly mention that they’re “going through a body change.” Then, as the kids get older, they can talk more openly about what they’re experiencing, says Dr. Dweck. Encouraging their children to ask questions about menopause can also build empathy and normalize conversations surrounding health.

On the flip side, Parker wants Gen Z women to pay attention to what their mothers are going through, and not wait until the right moment to spark a conversation. “Having those conversations with my mom has made that feel a lot less scary and a lot more human,” she says. “Every stage of life comes sooner than you think, so it’s worth paying attention to your health long before you feel like you have to.”

Cancio didn’t feel like she could have those conversations with her mom, which is part of what inspired her to start making content around women’s health topics for younger women. “I started thinking about the girl who was sitting at home Googling something because she was too embarrassed to ask her mom, or the girl who thought something was wrong with her because nobody had ever explained that what she was experiencing was normal,” she says.

Even though the way that Gen Z is learning about menopause isn’t perfect—whether through a viral post or their mother—it’s still a step in the right direction. By doing her part, Cancio hopes to have a completely different relationship with her future daughter “where no topic about her body is off limits and she never feels like she has to search for answers alone.”

#4813. How to Prevent Arguments at Thanksgiving Dinner

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

The days leading up to Thanksgiving can feel like a whirlwind. Between figuring out who’s bringing what and dodging holiday traffic, nerves can wear thin before the first guest arrives. The extra leaf has to be wrestled out of the closet to stretch the table a little longer, and someone has been up since dawn coaxing the turkey toward golden. By the time everyone sits down, the coats are piled high on a bed down the hall and someone is sneaking a roll before grace. Then, somewhere between the first helping and the pie, a loaded remark cuts across the table and the tension becomes palpable. We spend weeks preparing the meal, yet the conversations shared over it rarely receive the same forethought.

Over the years, journalists have asked me how to keep Thanksgiving conversations from boiling over, and I always say we can’t control what others say or do, but we can choose how we respond. The key is remembering the person across the table matters more than proving a point.

Before the gathering, it helps to take inventory of ourselves. I think of it like packing for a trip somewhere new. We check the forecast and pack for the weather we expect, knowing the skies can still shift once we land. In the same way, we can reflect on which topics might feel sensitive this year.

If some relatives tend to bring up challenging subjects, a quick heads-up can make those conversations easier to navigate. We might say, “I’ve been looking forward to being together, and it would mean a lot if we could keep things lighter this year.” Sharing this means everyone can arrive on the same page and enjoy one another’s company.

Thanksgiving conversations have a way of wandering into topics no one meant to open. A comment lands the wrong way and suddenly we’re deciding whether to let it go or respond. A racing heart can be a cue to take a breath and pause. In that pause, we can ask ourselves three questions:

These questions can help us decide how, if at all, to engage. If the answer to any of them is no, we can steer the conversation toward common ground. We don’t have to follow every conversation into the weeds. Sometimes the kindest thing we can do for a conversation is to decide not to have it.

At the same time, steering clear of hard topics isn’t always the answer. A difficult conversation doesn’t have to strain our relationships. Research on Thanksgiving discussions suggests that college students whose families encouraged open conversation reported more positive effects on family closeness and less stress afterward.

A disagreement does not have to become an argument. Much depends on whether we are trying to prove a point or to understand someone. Scholarship on serial arguments indicates that people often care more about working things out together than gaining the upper hand. Arguments tend to take hold once difference feels like a threat, pulling us into an either/or mindset where one view must prevail over the other. To stay on the side of understanding, we can ask ourselves, “How can I express my views while still showing respect and valuing this person?” If a conversation feels uncomfortable, we might say, “I hear you, and I hold a different perspective.” Sentiments like these help others feel heard, even when we see things differently.

Of course, it wouldn’t be Thanksgiving without someone bringing up that topic—the one half the family has been hoping to avoid. We try to change the subject, and for a few minutes the conversation moves on to football and Black Friday deals. Then, just as everyone relaxes, that same relative finds a way back to the topic. It’s understandable to feel frustrated, yet shutting down the conversation can create more distance. After all, this is someone who matters to us, and there may be something more going on beneath the surface.

Difficult conversations can be complex webs of unspoken needs and hidden emotions. Maybe our relative is trying to make sense of something they’re going through, or looking for connection without knowing how to express that need. They may feel anxious or unheard. Or, there may be reasons we haven’t considered at all.

Without fully knowing the reason, some thoughtfulness can go a long way. It’s worth considering the experiences that may be influencing their viewpoint. Stepping into another’s shoes, even for a moment, can foster understanding and empathy. Offered sincerely, an affirmation such as “I can tell how much you care about this” conveys they are seen and heard, which can change the tone of the whole conversation.

Other times, we watch from the sidelines as two relatives barrel toward an argument we all saw coming. Family arguments often gain momentum through the quick volley of replies, each one arriving a little faster and a little louder than the last. Before long, the momentum takes over in ways the original comment never would have on its own.

In situations like these, we can interrupt the pace, not the people. A calm invitation such as “This feels a little tense. Maybe we can pause this for now” can slow things down, and families tend to respond more openly to understanding than to judgment. Asking a relative to help carry dishes to the kitchen or check on the pie breaks the rhythm without putting anyone on the spot, giving each person a graceful way to step back with their dignity intact. The goal isn’t to referee or get everyone to agree, but to give the whole table a chance to reset.

Keeping the peace at Thanksgiving doesn’t require everyone to share the same point of view, and understanding someone else’s doesn’t mean giving up our own. We can, however, choose how we treat one another, even when we disagree.

Bevan, J. L. (2010). Serial argument goals and conflict strategies: A comparison between romantic partners and family members. Communication Reports, 23(1), 52–64. doi.org/10.1080/08934211003598734

Johnson, A. J., Bostwick, E. N., & Cionea, I. A. (2019). Talking turkey: Effects of family discussions about the 2016 election over the Thanksgiving holiday. Journal of Family Communication, 19(1), 63–76. doi.org/10.1080/15267431.2018.1543688

#4811. Hästens 2000T Mattress, Tested and Reviewed (2026)

From the moment I touched down in Sweden, the focus was on sleep. Coming off a red-eye flight from New York with only two hours of rest (three if we’re being generous), there was nothing more I wanted to do than lie down. Luckily, a Hästens mattress—the reason for my trip—awaited me at the hotel and soon provided what was perhaps the most luxurious nap I’d ever experienced.

The Swedish manufacturer, which has been making beds since 1852, sits atop the luxury market for mattresses. The brand—whose name is Swedish for “the horse’s”—has a consuming commitment to craftsmanship, and its horsehair-filled beds are handmade. That level of focus also comes with a hefty price tag, which is why the brand is perhaps best known by the general public for its presence in celebrity homes (or possibly its cameo in an Emily in Paris episode as the subject of the titular character’s latest marketing campaign). But reputation aside, Hästens knows how to make a damn good bed.

But what earns a mattress luxury status? And what is it actually like to sleep on one from Hästens? After touring the brand’s main factory in Köping, Sweden, I’ve laid my head on one of its most popular mattresses, the 2000T, for the last few months, all in the name of trying to understand how much money a good night’s sleep is worth.

To the average person, horsehair is likely not the first mattress fill material that comes to mind—if it comes to mind at all. Gel, innerspring, memory foam, cotton, or some combination of those are way more common. But horsehair has a historic precedent, having been used in beds for many periods of human history, particularly when horses were the primary mode of transportation.

Much of the present-day reason for using the material comes from a scientific point of view: Horsehair strands are naturally hollow, which Hästens claims “transports any excess heat and moisture from your body during deep sleep.” Additionally, when cut and treated, the strands form a helix shape, which works in conjunction with the metal springs in a bed for a strong base of support.

Exterior of the Hastens factory in Köping, Sweden, designed by British architect Ralph Erskine.

An hour and a half train ride northwest from Stockholm, the small town of Köping is so quiet, you might expect to see a horse roaming the streets—maybe having recently received a haircut to donate to the mattress cause. When thinking of the word factory, one may expect a loud, gigantic warehouse filled with whirring machines and assembly lines moving so quickly you can hardly see the product before it whizzes past. But the Hästens factory possessed a quite different vibe. Sure, there is still machinery and expansive production areas, but it was fairly quiet, and I felt that the energy was more akin to a pottery studio than an industrial plant: craft-forward, methodical, and with a focus on handmade artistry. In fact, my host told me that only around 100 people work in the main factory, most of whom are from the area, highlighting the company as a point of pride for the local community.

Walking into the processing room of the factory, I was greeted by a small mountain of horsehair on the floor. It looked much more like a soft version of steel wool than the shiny mane and tail I was envisioning. That’s because the hair is cut down to small strands prior to being integrated into the mattresses. The hair also goes through several disinfecting and processing treatments before it even arrives at the factory. Taking a clump between my hands, I was surprised by its springiness. (And horse girls need not fear about animal welfare: My host for the trip confirmed that their suppliers from farms around the world aren’t killing horses for their hair, the mane and tail cuttings they receive are ethically sourced.)

The blue check pattern, developed by fourth-generation company leader Jack Ryde in 1978, is synonymous with the brand. So much so that a check-laden Mercedes was waiting to drive us from the train station to the factory.

Each layer of horsehair in the mattress is fluffed by hand and placed between sheets of cotton and wool.

Every aspect of the bed creation process happens by hand: prepping the layers of wool and horsehair for the filling, arranging and securing steel springs, framing the Swedish pine base. I watched workers build each part of the bed with a devoted level of care. The only fully automated aspect of the bed manufacturing that I witnessed on my tour was stitching a pattern onto the top mattress to give it a signature tufted texture. But even that is hand-sewn on certain bed models.

Quality is tested at every step, and if something isn’t up to par, production restarts. For some models, including the Grand Vividus (at the top of Hästens range), there are only a select few craftspeople who are trained in the production process. Much of the brand’s higher price tag comes down to that heightened level of labor and care. If someone on the team is sick or is simply just working slower on a given day, the production timeline increases to accommodate the quality level that Hästens demands: perfection.

My loaned mattress also included a full set of Hästens bedding.

The 2000T is one of the brand’s best sellers, falling around the middle of their price range.

When it comes to my sleep setup, my mattress was the element that I’d been putting off upgrading for years. I only leveled up my years-old box spring with a mattress topper a few years ago. I tend to prioritize bedding when buying new duds for the bedroom, and because I’m consistently testing various sets of sheets for AD, my focus tends to be on how linens can visually transform a space rather than shift my physical experience. All to say, upgrading to a Hästens was like going from a hand-me-down sedan to a Lamborghini.

Before receiving the loaned mattress for testing, I tried out different models in person at the Manhattan flagship store in NoMad, an experience Hästens coins the Sleep Spa. As a staff member talked me through proper spinal alignment and important pressure points, I lay on various models in a Goldilocks-esque journey to see which mattress was the right fit. True to Hästens’ superlative level of service, even this part of the process felt curated. Ambient music played, lights dimmed, and I was given two pillows and a duvet for snuggling. The meditative process made me focus on how my body responded to each mattress. As a combination stomach-and-side sleeper—and someone who likes to sit on her bed—I selected the 2000T (in firm) after around an hour of sampling.

Despite being a firmer model, the 2000T still contours to my body in a way that I can only describe as cushy. The horsehair filling provides a unique springiness that the compression of memory foam or cotton can’t quite replicate. It sinks in just enough to give my shoulders enough space when I sleep on my side, but is supportive enough to keep my hips from dropping out of alignment for the nights I’m on my stomach.

As I mentioned, I often lounge on bed to read, play video games, or what have you. While facilitating sleep is the primary function of a mattress, I was keen to see how its edge control and support would stand up to this alternative usage. I was surprised by how little back pain I sustained after reading sessions that extended beyond two hours. Because of its reinforced springs at the corners and edges, I could also sit right on the edge of the mattress without feeling like I was going to roll off.

The aspect of the horsehair fill I was most intrigued to test was its claim of moisture and heat-wicking properties. I like to be fully swaddled underneath my duvet, top sheet, and sometimes even another blanket when I sleep, which can be a recipe for waking up sweaty. That hasn’t happened once with the 2000T. The foam topper on my prior bed often trapped heat, and I’d wake up in the middle of the night to rip off some of the layers of bedding in order to cool down. With the Hästens, though, I can be as greedy with my bedding as I want to be without overheating.

The ‘massage’ portion lasted about 10 minutes.

As part of their high bar of customer service, the company offers a free recalibration program from select stores to help maintain the longevity of the mattress and mitigate any compression issues. The product care program involves Hästens staffers visiting your home (typically once a year) to flip and massage the mattress—the latter consisting of a person marching back and forth across the mattress to redistribute the fill materials. I can safely say having a grown man in booties walk in circles on top of my bed for 10 minutes was one of the oddest moments of my life, but sleeping on the bed that night, I could feel the difference. While there weren’t any severe lumps formed in my two-month testing period, the process smoothed out any compression in the areas I most often lay.

Although I’ve only slept on the 2000T for around two months, I can see a noticeable change in how my body feels after a night’s rest. I struggle with hypermobility and have a family history of arthritis, so I’m on high alert about how my joints feel upon waking up in the morning. On my old bed, I typically awoke with some pain in my hips and a stiff lower back. While sleeping on the Hästens hasn’t fully eliminated any achiness, I essentially ceased needing to do the typical stretching routine I used to perform in the morning in order to get my body ready for the day.

Down pillows were provided by the brand for my loaner bed.

The structure of Hästens beds includes a top mattress and middle mattress, the former mimicking a thick topper.

As someone who has notoriously bad nighttime habits (like plentiful screen time), I had accepted I’d only be able to expect a low level of restfulness from my sleep. I was content with a solid six hours and low-level of back achiness in the morning, thinking I couldn’t consistently adjust my routine to improve my experience. Sleeping on the Hästens 2000T has changed that mindset drastically. It’s without a doubt the best mattress I’ve ever slept on.

However, it’s easy for me to say this bed is worth it because I didn’t have to pay the steep price tag of $74,780 to try it out in my home. Yes, Hästens exceeded my expectations when it came to sleep, but after the testing period ends, I don’t anticipate a sudden change in my finances that would allow me to invest in my own 2000T. Although the brand’s beds are built to last a lifetime, and we spend a third of our lives asleep, the question of how much a good night’s sleep is really worth is highly individualized.

This experience more broadly made me consider where we are most willing to invest in when it comes to our home spaces. Sure, a covetable mattress like one from Hästens may not be as flashy as other big-ticket purchases, like a giant flat screen, but I’d posit a splurge has few better use cases than on something you return to each night.

#4809. Tennis is Aces for Healthy Aging

There’s good reason why the United States Tennis Association calls it “the world’s healthiest sport.”

If we told you tennis has been shown to boost heart health, balance, strength, mental acuity, and mood plus add nearly 10 years to your life, you might think we also had a bridge to sell you. But it’s true: Research shows that even recreational tennis can have a seriously impressive impact on your health—now and for years to come.

“Tennis is a whole-body sport,” says sports medicine surgeon Alexis Colvin, MD, chief medical officer of the US Open. “It offers cardiovascular benefits, muscle strengthening, flexibility—all the things you need to deal with any physical challenges later in life.”

You also don’t have to be a star tennis player to reap the longevity benefits, Dr. Colvin adds. In a 2020 study she co-authored, researchers surveyed over 10,000 tennis players, most of them recreational; about 70 percent played just one to three days a week. The players scored higher than the general population on measures such as physical strength, mental and emotional health, and social engagement. “You don't have to be playing at a very high level to get those benefits,” Dr. Colvin says.

And those benefits appear to extend one’s life: When researchers followed 8,577 people for up to 25 years, they found that those who played tennis an average of 103 minutes a week lived 9.7 years longer than their sedentary counterparts. They also lived significantly longer than cyclists (who get an extra 3.7 years), swimmers (3.4 years), and joggers (3.2 years).

Even if you’ve never played tennis before, it’s never too late to start. Keep reading for five reasons to pick up a racket, hit the court, and do your future self a favor.

Tennis involves bursts of high intensity movement—sprinting to the net, running backwards to lob a volley, stopping and then lunging to the opposite side of the court to hit the ball—all of which can do wonders for your cardiovascular health. It boosts heart rate, maximizes your body’s use of oxygen, strengthens heart muscle, improves circulation, and can lower blood pressure and cholesterol levels. As a result, women who play tennis an average two to three hours a week have a 44 percent lower risk of developing cardiovascular disease and a 66 percent lower chance of dying from it.

When you sprint across the court, swing a racquet, or come to a sudden stop, you’re working your leg muscles, core, shoulders, back, and arms—in other words, strengthening nearly every part of the body. A recent study of more than 5,000 women between the ages 63 and 99 found that those who had greater muscle strength lived the longest. And because you’re also supporting your own body weight as you run and land, the sport also helps increase bone density, Dr. Colvin says. Stronger bones mean a lower risk of fractures and osteoporosis in the future, which is what you need if you want to age well.

Tennis requires coordinated movement and muscle control to maintain fluid footwork and smooth, continuous swings. Your core helps make that possible and is key to good balance. Both core strength and balance can help you avoid falls and fractures as you get older. Another part of balance is visuospatial skill—the ability to recognize environmental cues that help you stay upright. Tennis may help sharpen that, too. In a 2022 study, older tennis players who faced a disruption that could throw them off balance were able to react and steady themselves as well as younger players.

Tennis demands intense focus and decision making. “There’s a lot of active thinking going on,” Dr. Colvin says. “You’re making a lot of split-second decisions while you’re playing, plus thinking about the overall strategy of the game. That kind of mental engagement is important as we get older.” According to research, engaging in that kind of quick and strategic thinking while being physically active may be particularly good at promoting neuroplasticity and boosting cognitive function—both of which can stave off the cognitive decline that can come with age.

Studies have found that people who play tennis regularly tend to be less stressed or anxious than people who do lower-intensity exercise. They also report feeling more optimistic, less depressed, and a greater sense of well-being. Like other high-energy sports, tennis may boost mood by prompting the release of brain chemicals such as endorphins, dopamine, and serotonin. It’s also a fun game to play with friends. “The social aspect of tennis is one of its key benefits,” Dr. Colvin says. Numerous studies show that those kinds of community ties are essential for a long, healthy, happier life. With tennis, that’s built into the game.

#4808. Bye-Bye, Beige! This 517-Square-Foot Apartment Became a Creative Retreat Full of Light and Color

“My previous home was dominated by shades of beige,” Jaco Kroon says. “And it no longer suited me.” After a career in marketing, Kroon decided to head in a different direction and devote himself to a new creative pursuit: designing furniture for pets. He found the perfect setting for this fresh start in a 517-square-foot apartment in Amsterdam. Together with Elza Wandler, a designer and founder of her eponymous accessory brand, he created an interior that reflects his evolving vision. “I wanted a place that underscores my new direction—a more colorful, more creative, and more surprising home,” explains Kroon.

A vase by ceramist Pol Chambost brings contrast to the table.

“I’d seen a few articles about Elza Wandler’s home and immediately thought: That’s exactly the kind of environment I want: creative, personal, and full of objects that tell stories,” Kroon recalls. What began as creative interest soon developed into a friendship. During a lunch together in the designer’s garden, the two hit it off right away. In addition to their passion for interior design, they also share a love of dogs—they both own poodles.

As Kroon got to know Wandler’s home better, he was particularly struck by the fact that every object had its own unique character. They wanted to create a similar atmosphere in his apartment, which led to a close creative collaboration in which they both contributed their ideas and visions. For Kroon, his home soon became more than just a place to live: “While the work was underway, I was developing my own line of pet furniture and realized just how much the new interior was influencing my creative work as well.”

Jaco Kroon’s love for animals has come to shape his career. He’s seen here with his faithful toy poodle, Elio.

The biggest challenge of the project was making the best use of the limited space. The 517-square-foot apartment combines a kitchen, living room, dining area, and sleeping area without feeling cramped or having to make any sacrifices. According to Wandler, the key was to view the spaces as a cohesive ecosystem: “In such small spaces, every single object interacts with the others. Even a four-inch-tall vase can completely alter the balance of a room.”

The bedroom is decorated in shades of salmon, with custom cabinets framing the bed. The wallpaper is by Kelly Wearstler. Wall sconces by Contain and the bedding is by Bonsoirs.

This gave rise to the project’s motto: “Every item must be a Beyoncé”—that’s how Wandler and Kroon jokingly describe their design philosophy. It’s their way of expressing the idea that every piece should bring its own personality and presence to the home without disrupting the harmony of the environment. The color scheme also follows this principle with intense yet carefully coordinated tones—such as the eggplant in the kitchen and the warm, velvety salmon pink in the bedroom—paired with textured woods, vintage fabrics, and custom details. “At first, the idea of a burgundy-violet kitchen really put me off,” Kroon admits with a smile. “But the further we got into the project, the more I felt my horizons expanding.”

A blue bowl by Wandler x SolidNature and a ceramic basket by Ferm Living add splashes of color to the burgundy kitchen. The art on the wall is by Laura de Wilde.

One distinctive feature of the project is the interplay between functionality and aesthetics: Practical solutions blend so naturally into the design that they are barely recognizable as such at first glance. The historic Amsterdam townhouse, with its large windows, had very little storage space. That’s why Wandler took advantage of nearly every opportunity to create additional storage solutions. Custom cabinets frame the bed like an architectural backdrop, while the TV disappears into a specially designed piece of furniture made of zebrawood.

“Elza has turned what would normally be a purely functional piece of furniture into something beautiful. She even convinced me to hide the TV behind the doors of a zebrawood cabinet!” jokes Kroon. “Everything seems to have been designed for aesthetic reasons, but in fact, every element is tailored to make optimal use of the available space.” The decision to use zebrawood also follows this philosophy: Its striking grain lends the interior a vertical dynamism and makes the room appear more spacious. “I wanted to use the wood to create movement and depth,” explains Wandler. “In a small room, you always have to consider how to increase the sense of space.”

Colorful accents, such as the stool by Rutger de Regt, make a bold statement in the interior. The vase is by India Mahdavi and the sculpture on the wall is by Floor Merjenburgh.

As is often the case with Wandler’s projects, restored vintage pieces, contemporary design, and works by young artists all find a place side by side here. The large vintage sofa was completely reupholstered, while the artwork and decorative pieces come from a network of emerging designers and artists supported by the designer through Kamer—her curatorial platform dedicated to collectible design.

The dark wood of the floor complements the chocolate-brown armchair by Norr11.

“It’s important to me that I feel happy in my home,” says Kroon. “And that it stimulates creativity.” Wandler sought to create this feeling through her selection of artwork and a carefully coordinated lighting design. The latter plays a central role in the living concept: Since the apartment faces multiple directions, the natural light changes constantly throughout the day, causing colors and materials to appear different depending on the time. This creates the impression that this small apartment was conceived as a place that evolves and can accompany personal transformation; it embraces new ideas, new ambitions, and new identities. “The greatest compliment,” Wandler concludes, “was when Jaco said to me, ‘Now I feel like I’m finally living as the version of myself that I want to become.’”

The dining area, with a table from Westwing, is connected to the living room. The vintage sofa by Cini Boeri for Arflex has been reupholstered; the vase in front of the window is by l’Objet.

From fashion-forward watches to tough outdoor timepieces, we found the best watches for every budget.

Take Koon's gold watch in Pulp Fiction or 007's high-tech timepieces: The best watches for men tell a story and time, while instantly elevating your ensemble. Need a leather-strapped dress watch that pairs nicely with your suit? Or maybe you're after a rugged outdoor watch or sports watch to track your laps?

With many options on the market, finding the right one can feel like diving into a black hole. But don't sweat it—we've tested it all, from everyday essentials to luxury standouts. Whether you're looking to monitor your fitness stats, are after your first watch to wear to the office, need some water-resistance, or have to have dial luminescence in the dark for easy readability, these 7 watches have proven to be the best in style, durability, and function. Step right up, because there's a watch for every guy.

Timex offers the ultimate bang-for-your-buck watch, no question about it. Our testers found it’s the easiest dial to read of all the watch options on this list. That lively blue is sharp enough to catch everyone’s attention but still versatile enough to pair with pretty much any casual or formal fit. It fits comfortably on the wrist and can smoothly adjust if you need to loosen or tighten it. And here’s the kicker: It’s under $100.

Yep, you get all this without putting a dent in your wallet—which can be said for nearly all the watches Timex makes. At the push of the crown, the brand's signature Indiglo light-up feature will take over, which means no squinting to see the time for both daytime strolls and late-night outings. The two-tone silver and brass case and mineral glass crystal keep it durable yet lightweight, so it can handle daily wear. Plus, with 10 different colorways, there are options to match your vibe, whether you want something that is "in your face" or semi-low-key.

Read More: The Best Amazon Watches for Men

Seiko delivers a solid mashup of modern and vintage flair in its special edition 5 Sports timepiece. Pulling inspo from the post-war racing boom of the 1960s, the watch dons a checkered flag bezel design, which is not something you see every day. The black dial continues the retro vibes with a white and black checkered circle to frame the indices for the numbers. We also love the red-orange second hand that adds a fun pop of color and harkens back to racing watches and timers of the post-war era.

Flip it over, and you’ve got a see-through caseback that lets you peek at the Caliber 4R36 movement—always a cool feature for anyone who loves the horology. We found it has some significant weight to it, but feels balanced and secure on the wrist. It’s an automatic watch, which means no batteries—you just wear it, and it powers itself through your every movement (approximately 41 hours of power reserve). Another bonus: It’s priced at a level that won’t make your wallet cry, which is a steal for the quality you’re getting—something Seiko has become known for.

Attention athletes and adventurers: The G-Shock G-LIDE is loaded with features that keep a record of your progress. First, this bad boy connects to a smartphone app that tracks tides at thousands of beaches, so it’s perfect for surfers, swimmers, or anyone who spends more time in the water than on land. I’ve used it at the pool during the summer, and it crushed it—handled constant splashes without a hiccup, shrugged off chlorine like it was nothing, and the resin strap stayed super comfortable even when wet. Not to mention, timing my laps was a total breeze. All to be expected for the legendary durability of G-Shocks.

In terms of fit, this one islarger, and on smaller wrists, it might look oversized or feel bulky. However, it's an athletic watch, so you'll probably be in workout shirts and not have to worry about fitting it under shirt cuffs.

All things considered, the G-Shock G-LIDE is brimming with other functions that track your laps, cadence, and pace—advantageous for runners, rowers, or gym-goers looking to crush their 2026 (and forthcoming 2027) goals. It’s designed to handle impacts (like any G-Shock), whether you’re wiping out on a wave or accidentally dropping it during a workout. I also found the LED backlight makes it super easy to read in low-light conditions, especially during a late-night jog. Other practical elements include a full auto-calendar, an energy-saving feature to keep the battery going strong, and a design that delivers durability and performance in one.

When it comes to field watches, the Hamilton Khaki Field is the gold standard—simple, robust, and packed with style. Speaking of which, the cool blue dial of this version, paired with the brushed steel case, gives it a clean, understated look that’s perfect for everyday wear. At 38mm, it’s compact and classic, sitting just right on your wrist without feeling too bulky.

Recreating the 1960s soldier watch, it’s a timepiece that nails that balance between functionality and style—you could wear it while exploring the outdoors or just heading to a casual dinner. The Super-LumiNova coating on the hands and markers is a game-changer, ensuring the watch is legible in low light or total darkness. We've put it to use during a camping trip and it lit up like a champ when the campfire died down, making it easy to check the time without fumbling for a flashlight. And just last year, Hamilton came out with a quartz version of the KF that's even more affordable and offers the ease of quartz.

The Bremont Terra Nova is the kind of watch that effortlessly blends rugged practicality with standout style. The cushion-shaped case? It’s got a cool military-meets-modern vibe that makes it stand out without trying too hard. Pair that with the rich green and black striped NATO strap, and you’ve got a watch that screams adventure but still looks sharp enough to wear out on the town.

As for the automatic movement, it features a Glucydur balance wheel (enhances its precision by maintaining consistent oscillations), an Anachron balance spring (offers excellent resistance to magnetic fields), and a Nivaflex mainspring (stores 38 hours of energy to power the watch).

What really makes it a go-to for adventurers and aviators is the oversized Super-LumiNova numerals. These bad boys light up like a beacon, so whether you’re navigating a trail at sunset or checking the time mid-flight in low light, you’ll always have clear visibility. It’s built for people who don’t just sit still—this is a watch designed to keep up with your wildest days and nights while keeping you looking sharp.

The Tudor Black Bay isn’t just any watch—it’s the perfect blend of timeless style, top-notch craftsmanship, and everyday usability. Let’s start with that 41mm steel case. The polished and brushed finish gives it that sophisticated edge while staying tough enough to manage the wear and tear of daily life. Paired with a black rubber strap, it strikes the perfect balance: sporty yet versatile, rugged yet refined. In other words, you could take it to the boardroom, the beach, or the mountains and it’ll look right at home. Not to mention, the strap has a slimmer profile and slightly textured feel that grips your wrist just enough without being sticky or uncomfortable. It's not overly thick or flimsy, and it doesn't soak water or sweat.

Tudor is known for its no-nonsense approach to legibility, and we found the Black Bay is no exception. It’s bold and clean, with luminous markers that practicality glow in low light. So whether you’re checking the time in a dimly lit bar or on an overnight hike, it’s always easy to read. Most mechanical watches offer approximately between 36 and 48 hours, but this one takes it up a level with a 70-hour power reserve. Overall, it’s the kind of watch that will still feel relevant and stylish 20, 30, and even 50 years down the road.

If you’re ready for any action-packed adventure—007 style—the Omega Seamaster Diver 300m is the watch you want. This model is the exact one Bond wears in "No Time to Die," so you know it’s got that "mission-ready" vibe. It’s super lightweight, made from titanium, and has a matching titanium mesh bracelet, so it’s built to last and handle anything—from magnetic fields to pressure underwater. Plus, it even has a Helium escape valve—a small pressure-release system that lets tiny built-up gas particles flee to prevent the crystal from popping off.

During our testing, we noticed the titanium bracelet feels incredibly light on the wrist, which makes a big difference for all-day comfort. It has a smooth, almost silky texture but isn't as glossy. Another bonus: Titanium is hypoallergenic, so it won't irritate the skin for people with metal sensitivities.

This watch is a serious upgrade and, yeah, it’s the priciest one on the list, but here’s why it’s worth the investment: It’s a timeless classic with next-level features that will last a lifetime. It’s powered by the Chronometer 8806 movement, so it’s super accurate, and it comes with a 5-year warranty, just in case. In all honesty, it's the kind of watch that'll make you look like a million bucks at an upscale gala or extravagant dinner party. Pair it with a tailored suit and some slick dress shoes for a look that means business.

The movement is the engine of the watch—it's what keeps it ticking. Below, we've broken down the main three types and their benefits.

Powered by a battery and known for being super accurate, quartz movement is low maintenance, lightweight, and affordable. It's a great option if you just want a reliable watch without the fuss. Quartz watches will only require the replacement of the battery every few years, which is a simple task and costs fairly little.

Backed by the motion of your wrist—no battery required. The gears that make up the movement wind themselves when the watch moves. Automatic watches feel a little more special, sometimes like high-end brands Rolex or Omega, but they'll need to be worn regularly or placed in a watch winder to stay powered. They'll also require consistent maintenance and servicing to keep them optimally running. Automatic watches typically cost more than most quartz watches, but there are many great options that are affordable these days.

You wind it yourself, usually every couple days. Instead of the movement rotating automatically with motion, the gears need hand-winding to keep the movement running. These watches require attention and typically harken back to the era of vintage, throwback timepieces like pocket watches. Manual watches usually cost more than quartz watches and are on par in price with some automatic watches. They tend to be a little less affordable though.

Think of the case as the body of the watch—it's the shell that houses everything important, like the movement (the engine that makes it tick) and the dial (the thing with the numbers and hands). Cases come in different shapes, sizes, and materials. Below, we break down the most common materials used for cases.

Durable, versatile, and scratch-resistant. It's the most common and works for everyday wear.

Lighter than steel but just as strong, making it perfect for sports watches.

Scratch-proof and sleek but can be a bit pricey. It has a modern, luxurious feel.

A strap is any flexible band—made of leather, rubber, nylon, or fabric—that secures the watch to your wrist. Straps can change the entire vibe of the watch. A bracelet, on the other hand, is made of metal—stainless steel, titanium, or sometimes gold—linked together. Bracelets usually feel sturdier and add a bit of weight to the watch, giving a more premium, polished look. The good thing is many watches allow you to swap between a strap and a bracelet, so you can switch up the style depending on the occasion.

Classic, comfortable, and stylish. Perfect for dress watches but less durable for heavy-duty activities.

Stainless steel or titanium bracelets are durable and versatile for both casual and formal occasions.

Great for sports and water activities—comfortable and easy to clean.

When shopping for the best men's watch, features and complications can make all the difference in terms of functionality and style. Ultimately, these details should match your lifestyle. We've broken down some important specs to keep an eye out for, but these are by no means an exhaustive list of everything you could find in some complex watches.

This is the ring around the watch face, and when it rotates, it actually serves a purpose (beyond looking cool). On dive watches, for example, the bezel is used to track elapsed time—turn it to line up with the minute hand before you dive, and you'll know how long you're underwater. Some bezels work for other things, like GMT watches, where they help track a second time zone. But in everyday life, most people just fidget with them because it's oddly satisfying with a ratcheting sound.

Water resistance tells you how well your watch can handle moisture. There are two equivalent measurements you will typically find when it comes to this rating. Meters (as in depth) is the first and atmosphere (designated as ATM and measures the pressure of every 10 meters. So the first rating is 30m, which is rated at 3 ATM. This is splash-proof, which means your watch can handle occasional hand-washing or light rain, but don't submerge it. 50m (5 ATM) is good for shallow water activities like light swimming, but no diving. 100m (10 ATM) can handle swimming, snorkeling, and most water sports. 200m+ (20 ATM) is built for diving and serious water activities. Watches like the Omega Seamaster are built specifically for this sort of pressure.

A chronograph is a type of complication added to the watch movement that essentially gives the watch a stopwatch functionality. It's great for timing events, workouts, or even laps around a track. You'll typically see sub dials for seconds, minutes, and sometimes hours. While it adds functionality, it also gives the watch a sporty, complex look. The most famous example of a chronograph is the Rolex Daytona, made famous by watch icon Paul Newman.

A date window adds convenience—you won't have to check your phone or calendar to know the date. It's a small but handy detail, especially for busy schedules. Watches such as the Seiko 5 or Tudor Black Bay makes this feature feel seamless by blending it into the design.

Luminous markers or hands are a must if you plan on wearing the watch in low-light situations, like at night or in darker environments. Watches with Super-LumiNova or tritium tubes glow brightly and for extended periods and make the dial easier to read when overhead light is sparse.

Pay attention to case diameter and thickness. Case diameter is the main number you'll see alongside watches. Generally speaking, around 38-42mm diameter is ideal for most wrists, but larger or smaller watches can suit personal taste. The diameter of cases tends to ebb and flow with watch trends. For the first part of this century, case sizes gravitated over 40mm for lots of watch makers. But in 2026, smaller watches (even down to 32 and 34mm) are en vogue. We like to find a happy medium and suggest trying on different sizes to see what's most comfortable for your wrist.

If you’re rough on your gear or are looking for an everyday wear, opt for a scratch-resistant sapphire crystal (the transparent covering that protects the dial), shock resistance, or robust designs for long-lasting wear.

Our style team, led by Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan, continually tests almost every watch known to man and put them through their paces for everything they’re designed to handle: marathon training, cycling, traveling, hiking, sleep tracking, daily fitness routines, and dressy occasions. To identify the most ubiquitous watches, we relied on our previous experience testing and owning various models, as well as prior expert coverage on Men’s Health.

We considered features such as case material, comfort, battery life, accuracy, dial design and aesthetics, water resistance, and magnetic resistance. Bonus points were given for unique specs that added functionality like a date window or sub dials. Our picks aren't just utilitarian though—they're seriously stylish, making them the perfect accessory for everything from the gym to date nights. In the end, we narrowed it down to 7 standout watches that tick all the right boxes and can provide a timepiece for any type of guy.

#4805. Elvis Presley at Home: Tour the King’s Private Life in 14 Photos, From the Heartland to Hawaii

Elvis Presley is one of those icons so permanently etched into the fabric of American popular culture that it seems, nearly half a century after his death, as if he will live forever. While Presley also had homes in California, and famously lived in Germany during his stint in the US Army, it is Graceland that is most strongly associated with the late musician. The rock and roller’s Memphis residence where he lived for 20 years and where he died at the age of 42, Graceland is America’s second-most-visited residence, behind the White House. Every year, an average of 600,000 people flock to the residence turned museum, which opened to the public in 1982.

Today, the museum, which encompasses Presley’s gravesite, former home, and a collection of mementos of Presley’s rock-and-roll career, stands as a stirring reminder of one man’s life, as he grew from a beloved child to poverty-stricken parents to, arguably, the most famous man in the world. Below, we’re rounding up photos of the legendary musician at his (almost) equally famous home, and other places he rested his pompadoured head.

The Presleys at home in Tupelo, around 1945

Presley and his parents pose for a photo at home in Tupelo, Mississippi, circa 1945—the year before he received his first guitar. The future king of rock and roll was born nearby, in a two-room house built by his father, grandfather, and uncle on January 8, 1935. That house, now a museum, was repossessed three years later, and the family bounced around other homes in the area before moving to Memphis when Presley was 13 years old. There, the family lived in Lauderdale Courts, a public housing project.

In March 1956, riding high on the success of Presley’s first RCA single, “Heartbreak Hotel,” the family became homeowners for the very first time. A house of her own had always been Gladys’s dream, and her 21-year-old son made it a reality when he paid $29,250 for 1034 Audubon Drive, a low-rise, seven-room ranch house with four bedrooms. Gladys likened it to living in a palace. They also added a backyard pool–at the time, it was the only one on the street. While most wealthy men of his tender age might have set their parents up with a house before shimmying off to live the bachelor’s life elsewhere, this wasn’t Elvis’s style; living together as a close-knit trio was always part of his master plan.

Elvis Presley and a friend chat in the back yard of his house at 1034 Audubon Drive in 1956.

On their quiet, leafy street in the rapidly growing East Memphis, the Presleys were soon living the suburban dream. Things might well have stayed that way too, had Elvis’s star not reached stratospheric heights over the following months. By the summer of 1956, Elvis had recorded smash hits “Hound Dog” and “Don’t Be Cruel.” His first feature film, Love Me Tender, premiered later that year, making him a bona fide movie star.

Elvis and his parents relax on the patio.

Elvis kicks his feet up alongside his parents on the Audubon Drive home’s patio in this July 1956 photo. The Presleys had moved to this upper-middle-class neighborhood just four months prior. During their residency, the family tried to fit in with their neighbors in the affluent community to the best of their ability; Gladys let local kids cool off in their newly installed pool and made them peanut butter sandwiches, while Elvis would take them for a spin on the back of his gleaming motorcycle. But it soon became clear that Elvis’s fame would put a strain on life in the area. Perhaps it was when Hollywood star Natalie Wood came to stay at the house on Audubon—which turned the street into a circus as fans gathered to watch her pose outside on Elvis’s motorcycle—or the hot dog stand that set up outside that magically appeared to feed the constant stream of fans. The final straw may have been when a helicopter landed on the vacant lot beside the house to collect Elvis, leaving the neighbors well and truly shaken up.

By March 1957 the Presleys had packed their bags and moved on from the house on Audubon, restoring a relative sense of peace to the quaint suburban neighborhood. The family may have spent just a year at their Audubon Drive home, but it was a pivotal chapter in Elvis’s life story, marking a transition between the transient lifestyle of his impoverished childhood and the security and permanence he would find in his next home: Graceland.

The new homeowner with his hand on one of Graceland’s now iconic columns.

Presley skyrocketed to stardom in the mid ’50s, garnering a recording contract with RCA Records. This newfound wealth meant the boy whose home was repossessed, and who lived in public housing, could now buy the lavish house of his dreams for himself and his parents. In March 1957, the 22-year-old “Hound Dog” singer paid $102,500 for Graceland, which would remain his primary residence for the rest of his life. The home had been built in 1939 on a plot of land the original owner named after his daughter, Grace; the name stuck. Here, Presley leans on one of the home’s pillars shortly after the purchase.

Elvis in wrought iron, and in the flesh, at the gates to Graceland.

The musician poses in front of Graceland’s famous wrought iron music note gate in April 1957, around the time he had it installed. Abe Saucer designed the gates—which feature life-size images of Elvis playing guitar amid musical notes—and had them custom-built by John Dillars Jr. At the time, the property spanned 13.8 acres, with the mansion clocking in at over 10,200 square feet—later, Elvis would expand it to 17,500 square feet and 23 rooms, with additions including the famous Jungle Room.

A palace fit for the king of rock and roll.

The “Burning Love” singer walks in front of Graceland, circa 1957. Early design details that Presley added to the Colonial Revival estate included a custom 15-foot-long blue metallic sofa (later reupholstered in white), a pink flagstone wall around the property, a kidney-shaped swimming pool, and a full-size soda fountain. In his initial renovations, Presley spent $500,000 (over $5 million in today’s dollars).

In March 1958, Presley was drafted into the US Army. He is pictured in his off-post home in Bad Nauheim, Germany, in January 1960, shortly after being promoted to sergeant. It was here that the 24-year-old singer met a 14-year-old Priscilla Beaulieu, when a friend of his who had spotted Priscilla at a restaurant brought her to a party at Presley’s place to introduce them. To this day, the home at 14 Goethestrasse is still a landmark for fans.

Elvis and his father mourning after the death of Gladys.

Elvis and his father Vernon on the steps of Graceland in August 1958, shortly after the deathof his beloved mother, Gladys. The two had been exceptionally close, and her loss was toprove a devastating turning point. Elvis had always believed that the purpose of his extraordinary success was to provide his parents with the security and comfort they had been denied during his childhood. Buying them a home, and ultimately one as grand as Graceland, had been central to that vision. But now, just as he had achieved everything he had worked for, his mother was gone. With the loss of her unwavering love and support, it was as though a curtain had fallen on Elvis’s life. The young man who had once seemed so certain of his place in the world would never quite be the same again.

In March, 1960, Presley was discharged from the Army and returned home to Graceland, but it was a sadder and lonelier place, since Gladys died while he was in basic training. Here, he stands with his Rolls-Royce in front of Graceland, circa 1960. The Jailhouse Rock star had an affinity for slick cars, but it wasn’t the only mode of transportation he enjoyed at the estate. Priscilla Beaulieu, who came to visit him at Graceland in 1962 and moved in the following year, wrote in her 1985 memoir Elvis and Me that he “turned Graceland into a private playground for us all. He’d have gun-shooting contests and also ‘screaming thrill rides’ when he’d pack several people into his custom-built golf cart and race around the grounds at top speed.”

Elvis and Priscilla were married in Las Vegas on May 1, 1967. He was 32; she was 21. Exactly nine months later, on February 1, 1968, their first and only child, Lisa Marie Presley, was born

Priscilla and Elvis brought a tropical design aesthetic home from their vacations in Hawaii.

Hawaii became a bit of a home away from home for Presley following his 1961 film, Blue Hawaii. He returned often to vacation there, including in 1968, when this snapshot was taken. The “Don’t Be Cruel” singer was so inspired by the tropical locale that he added a tiki-inspired space to Graceland. Now known as the Jungle Room, the kitschy den features wood-paneled walls, green shag carpeting on the floor and ceiling, carved wooden furniture with faux fur upholstery, and a built-in rock waterfall feature.

Priscilla, Elvis, and baby Lisa Marie relax at home.

The Presleys relax in Graceland’s pool area, circa 1970. He had added the kidney-shaped pool and flagstone patio to the property in 1957. This snapshot shares a relaxed, happy moment, but life with Elvis wasn’t all pool parties for Priscilla. In Elvis and Me, Priscilla wrote frankly about their controversial relationship: “When we met, I had just turned 14. The first six months I spent with him were filled with tenderness and affection. Blinded by love, I saw none of his faults or weaknesses. He was to become the passion of my life. He taught me everything: how to dress, how to walk, how to apply makeup and wear my hair, how to behave, how to return love—his way. Over the years he became my father, husband, and very nearly God.”

Elvis and Lisa Marie are shown here on the porch of Graceland in the early 1970s. Lisa Marie later recalled the curious rhythms of life at the mansion. Her father was nocturnal, she explained, and the household rarely got going before about two in the afternoon. Lisa Marie remembered fondly hearing the rotary phone ring and being summoned upstairs to spend quality time with her dad in his bedroom. “I would just sit up there, and he’d talk to me and ask what I was doing while he watched one of his 17 televisions or listened to records,” she said in her memoir, From Here to the Great Unknown, co-written with her daughter Riley Keough. On occasion, Elvis would come downstairs and take the family and their friends out for an impromptu evening at the movie theater, shutting it down so they could watch a James Bond film or The Pink Panther.
