#4802. Are You Experienced?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

I must achieve internal consistency. —Edmund Husserl, turning an Erlebnis (Type I experience) into an Erfahrung (Type II experience)

The gods decreed that I shall not be a translator, and I am grateful for that. A direct translation from one language to another is a goal we can strive for, but rarely attain fully. The words of any particular language are rich in unique shades of meaning, allusions, emotional undertones, and cross-references to synonyms, which live lives of their own.

Homer called his hero Odysseus πολύτροπος (polytropos), literally “a man of many turns.” But being “of many turns” does not call forth useful associations in English, and so translators have struggled with—and argued with each other about—what to make of polytropos. Some render the idea as “endlessly cunning” (Mitchell, 2014), while others prefer “complicated” (Wilson, 2018). Neither hits the mark. One might as well try shrewd, crafty, clever, or inventive. “Endlessly cunning” is marred by the addition of the adverb, and “complicated” makes it sound like Odysseus needs therapy. “Complex” would have been a better choice. I prefer the phrase “a man of many devices” (Murray, 1919), which recognizes Odysseus’s rich and variable toolbox of survival skills, including those involving deception.

Different languages emphasize and elaborate different concepts, whatever is important in their natural and cultural context. We can marvel at some of these differences. Since Franz Boas (1911) suggested the Greenland Inuit have four different words for snow, others have grown the list, while still others have declared Boas’s observation a myth, one they find vexingly persistent. Other inter-language differences are less controversial, and some of these refer to psychological states. How many types of love are there? The Hebrew tradition counts four. What kinds of longing are there? Is the Portuguese saudade equivalent to the German Sehnsucht? On Seinfeld, Kramer asks George if he has ever yearned. “Yearned?” George replies. “I’ve craved!”

Psychology can be understood as the science of behavior and experience. Both terms carry complexity, and the latter more so than the former. What, we ask, is an experience? It does not take a Ludwig Wittgenstein to see that this concept embraces many variants that may not even share a single common feature. To say that an experience is whatever one experiences is to kick the can down the road; it is a tautology.

When I asked A.I. Claude what an experience is, I received this response: “Experience (noun) has two main senses, and the difference matters.” Claude goes on to explain that one of these senses refers to a process or event, with a first-person involvement. A first kiss delivers this kind of experience. Another sense refers to accumulated knowledge or skill; the sort of thing you put on your résumé. The first sense is what is sometimes called lived experience, whereas the second sense goes further by demanding that something has been learned, something that contributes to the person’s σωφροσύνη (sophrosyne), or practical wisdom. Anyone can have a store of Type I (lived) experiences, but this does not make them “experienced.” The participle must be earned. To have lived experience may simply mean that one hasn’t died yet. To have Type II (empirical) experience means to have made active investments in life that can be cashed out to help reach one’s goals and enhance one’s well-being.

Explaining the conceptual difference between Type I and Type II experience in English requires space, patience, and some circumlocution. The German language offers a clean distinction between Erlebnis, ɛɐˈleːpnɪs, and Erfahrung, ɛɐ̯ˈfaːʁʊŋ. The difference between the two was elaborated by the philosophers Wilhelm Dilthey (1883) and Edmund Husserl (1900-1901), whose work is interesting to consider in light of today’s debates over epistemology (Krueger, 2026). Expressing a popular view, Aziz and Anjum (2025) suggest that the prevailing scientific ethos in psychology is limited and systematically biased by excluding, misrepresenting, and disadvantaging many human populations. What is silenced, according to this view, are the lived experiences existing in these populations. These lived experiences, it is further argued, must be given their due; they must be heard and respected. And so, the argument goes on, these lived experiences must be acknowledged as an alternative epistemology, a way of knowing things, a way of having “knowledges.” Authors arguing the line pursued by Aziz and Anjum differ in how far they wish to go. Some are willing to settle for a lived-experience epistemology being accepted as equivalent to the scientific theory-and-data epistemology. Others wish to see psychological science be remade in light of lived experiences. These writers view the traditional scientific epistemology as oppressive, colonialist, and exploitative.

Dilthey and Husserl would pause here. To them, Erlebnis (Experience Type I) and Erfahrung (Experience Type II) are equally essential to the human condition; they cannot be pitted against each other. What contemporary critics of conventional empirical science seem to miss is that Erlebnis cannot absorb Erfahrung. Being effortful, empirical, and hard-won, Erfahrung is the grounds for reasoned beliefs that can be put to the test, that can be modified or overturned by continued activity. Erfahrung remains a work in progress. An Erlebnis, by contrast, is registered, perhaps committed to memory, and then gradually lost. A tourist has Erlebnisse; a traveler gathers Erfahrungen. It is the difference between perception and cognition.

Science is Erfahrung tamed, structured, and refined into a systematic method. Well-designed studies are efficient ways of learning Nature’s secrets. We can have an Erlebnis when walking into the woods, but only by planting a garden, by experimenting with different seeds, and by pruning excess growth, can we come to have the kind of Erfahrung that allows us to explain things and to teach what we have learned. The rejection of science from the lived-experience perspective is a short-sighted endeavor. The most it can hope to achieve is a narrative. Listening to these narratives can be an Erlebnis, but what can it teach us?

Once the difference between the two types of experience is understood, many familiar narratives appear in a new light. An ancient myth tells us that Adam and Eve had lovely Erlebnisse in the Garden of Eden. In the Land of Nod, they were forced to make Erfahrungen. With that, they became self-aware.

Note: The image above shows what Claude produced when asked to capture the concept of lived experience visually. The effort is interesting but not entirely satisfying since there are several dimensions (time, space, meaning) cross-cutting a scheme built on the idea of concentricity. I confirm that I never use AI to do my writing for me.

Aziz, M. & Anjum G. (2025). Rethinking knowledge systems in psychology: addressing epistemic hegemony and systemic obstacles in climate change studies. Frontiers in Psychology, 16, Article 1533802. doi: 10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1533802.

Boas, F. (1911). Handbook of American Indian Languages, 1. Washington: Government Print Office. Smithsonian Institution, Bureau of American Ethnology, Bulletin 40.

Dilthey, W. (1883). Einleitung in die Geisteswissenschaften: Versuch einer Grundlegung für das Studium der Gesellschaft und der Geschichte [Introduction to the human sciences: An attempt to lay a foundation for the study of society and history] (Vol. 1). Duncker & Humblot.

Husserl, E. (1900–1901). Logische Untersuchungen [Logical investigations] (Vols. 1–2). Max Niemeyer.

Krueger, J. I. (2026). What it means to understand vs explain in psychology. Psychology Today Online. https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/one-among-many/202606/what-it-m…

Mitchell, S. (2014). The Odyssey - Homer. Washington Square Press.

Murray, A. T. (1919). The Odyssey – Homer. Putnam.

Wilson, E. (2018). The Odyssey - Homer. Norton.

#4801. How to Do the Walking Lunge for Lower Body Gains

Build stronger quads, hamstrings, and glutes one step at a time.

YOUR LEGS ARE built for movement, whether you’re running, walking, or jumping. So why do most go-to leg exercises have you planting your feet in one spot?

Enter the walking lunge, a truly dynamic lower-body exercise that’s a perfect complement to exercises like heavy squats and Romanian deadlifts. (A bonus: It’s a unilateral exercise that isn’t the dreaded Bulgarian split squat.) The walking lunge is one of the few strength moves that truly gets you moving. And in doing so, it exposes muscle imbalances, trains balance and coordination, and challenges your core and upper body more than you might expect—all while attacking every muscle in your legs.

Walking lunges might appear deceptively simple at first, especially if you have done standard reverse lunges before. And in truth, they can be simple. Here, Men’s Health fitness director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. walks you through the steps to take so that you’re not dragging your feet but making gains toward powerful legs.

FORM IS EVERYTHING with this move. You’ll want to stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, squeeze your glutes and shoulder blades while keeping your gaze at a neutral spot straight ahead of you.

Once you’re comfortable with this slow and controlled movement, you can add weights to build extra muscle and strength. You can hold them at your sides, hold them by your shoulders in what’s called a front rack position, or grab one heavy dumbbell and hold it to your chest in a goblet position. “Regardless of how you hold the load, make sure to keep your upper-body tight,” says Samuel. “Grip the dumbbells like you mean it, squeeze your shoulder blades, and tighten your abs, too.”

Don’t obsess over keeping your torso too upright, though, says Samuel. “Especially as you work with heavier loads, don’t be afraid to lean forward slightly,” he says. “That can help you capitalize on your glutes, one of your strongest muscle groups, with each stride.”

When you’re starting out, says Samuel, aim to take a step that keeps your front shin perpendicular to the ground when you lower your torso into the lunge. But as you grow more experienced, you can play with the length of your stride to chase different goals. “If you take very small steps forward,” says Samuel, “you’ll attack your quads more. Larger steps can help you build hip mobility and knee health. If you take larger steps, go lighter with the load.”

“The greatest benefits of the walking lunge come from how it challenges us while in motion,” says Samuel. “In addition to building strength and muscle, every step forward challenges your front leg (primarily tibailis and quad muscles) to decelerate your body in space, and then quickly work to accelerate into the next step. That’s building coordination and balance, in addition to training almost every lower-body muscle and building serious strength.”

You’ll work a number of major leg muscles when you do walking lunges, including your calves, hamstrings, quads, and glutes.

SMALL MISTAKES IN your walking lunge technique can turn the lower body exercise into a potential knee-wrecking disaster.

You want to land on the heel of your foot first to provide a strong base for the rest of your lunge position. When you get started with walking lunges, aim for a vertical shin as you lower down to the ground to stay at a 90-degree angle in your front and back legs.

You also don’t want to think of taking a step forward, but stepping out a couple inches by slightly turning your glute. Another adjustment to protect your knee is to shift your knee slightly outward instead of toward the midline. (If you still feel any knee pain during lunges, try a reverse lunge instead).

Keep your torso straight and avoid dipping forward, which you may be more inclined to do if you’re carrying heavy weights for this exercise. Your chest should be aligned with the back of your thigh the entire time. As you get up from the lunge, you want to avoid using momentum. That means no shoulder or torso rocking.

THE WALKING LUNGE is a great way to sneak in some movement on leg day if most of your lower-body exercises have both feet anchored to the ground. Load up some weights, and try to aim for 3 sets of 8 to 10 reps per leg, 1 to 2 times a week. You can alternate each leg or finish up all your reps on one leg before switching to the other. Samuel says that will keep more tension and gives you an opportunity to really focus on the muscle.

An advantage of this move is its versatility, allowing you to do it anytime, anywhere. If you’re crunched for time or in a hotel room, try bodyweight walking lunges. Do it for 45 seconds with a 15 second rest for 5 minutes to break a sweat and build muscle.

Jocelyn Solis-Moreira, MS is the associate health & fitness for Men's Health and has previously written for CNN, Scientific American, Popular Science, and National Geographic before joining the brand. When she's not working, she's doing circus arts or working towards the perfect pull-up.

Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., is the fitness director of Men's Health and a certified trainer with more than 10 years of training experience. He's logged training time with NFL athletes and track athletes and his current training regimen includes weight training, HIIT conditioning, and yoga. Before joining Men's Health, he served as a sports columnist and tech columnist for the New York Daily News.

#4800. 46 Host and Hostess Gifts to Get the Party Started (2026)

The good news is: You’re getting a free dinner. The bad news is: You’re now racking your brain for last-minute hostess gifts . Buying something nice for a host is a tricky affair—there’s no expectation to spend a lot of money, nor is there one to bring something other than a bottle of wine, really, but the people pleasers among us will resonate with this list (and our housewarming gifts write-up).

In our search for the most memorable and thoughtful gifts to buy when you’ve been invited anywhere, we located a range of fail-safe favorites: cordial glasses (a small cut above wine glasses), scented candles you really want for yourself, linen coasters—basically everything but the finishing salt (though that would’ve been a great addition…). Whether it’s a Christmas feast, a movie night, or just a casual aperitivo hour, stick with this roundup for the perfect hostess gift ideas.

The name says it all—showing up with one of these gifts is all but a guarantee you’ll be getting invited to every function to come. You won’t find benchwarmers anywhere on this list; every item in this category is truly an MVP. Highlights include a cookbook, a box of chocolate truffles, and an AD-team favorite in serveware from Lazy Jamie.

Those who suffer from short-term memory loss rely heavily on Amazon Prime memberships for that two-day turnaround. If you’re down to the wire and still in need of something thoughtful to deliver to your gracious host, these gifts will arrive as early as the next day. Throw a bow on these and no one will know you nearly forgot about your plans.

There’s no getting around it—this social situation is going to be weird for you, at least for the first 20 minutes. These unique hostess gifts will usher you into the in-group expeditiously, especially since they can use them as soon as this evening for serving dinner or dessert. If you secured an invite to their upstate cabin or beach cottage, you need to get something nice. Even if you received a last-minute invite, it’s always good form to bring a bottle of wine, an aperitif, or something to the dinner party. Lucky for you, we found related options that’ll show your hosts you were thinking of them—pieces for accentuating their bar cart or tabletop, like a tortoise print wine key or a fresh set of glasses.

Making a pit stop to your partner’s parents this holiday season? Armor yourself with an arsenal of thoughtful gift ideas to solidify your status as their favorite bonus child. Cut flowers send someone looking for a vase, but a beaded lily never needs one. With one of these thoughtful items in tow, we’re sure you’ll be welcomed back with open arms any time there’s a concert in town.

#4797. How a Former New York City Caviar Factory Became an Art-Filled Oasis of Calm

It’s late Friday afternoon in Manhattan and Alexis Piqueras has misplaced his phone. Not that he’s concerned. Bathed in the light of October’s early setting sun, the Spanish-born producer and founder of AP Studio, settles into a Charlotte Perriand dining chair at his Tribeca apartment. The vibe is calm: a mix of warm hues, rich textures, and timeworn woods. Candles perfume the air. And all around us the faces and limbs of figurative artworks seem to join our conversation. “I’ll find it eventually,” Piqueras notes, unperturbed by his absent device.

A break from our harried digital world was what he was seeking when, not long ago, he set out to buy an apartment downtown, having returned to New York after a three-year stint in Los Angeles. “Sometimes I need to hide amid the chaos,” says Piqueras, who has built a busy career collaborating with brands on the order of Louis Vuitton, Celine, and Loewe. His real-estate ambitions transcended any simple notions of an urban oasis. Yes, he wanted peace and quiet. But he also wanted some untouched architectural grit that felt true to the city, in particular his visions of its post-industrial 1970s waterfront.

Piqueras relaxes in the living area of his Manhattan loft with his dogs, Prince and Bridget; artworks by Wolfgang Tillmans (top) and Giangiacomo Rossetti.

A Harold Ancart painting and Prince preside over the entry.

Charlotte Perriand chairs and a custom sofa face off across an Alvar Aalto prototype cocktail table; floor lamp by Isamu Noguchi and seascape by Paul Thek.

He found that in Tribeca. Its warehouses and sleepy streets also reminded him of his time in Berlin, where he fell in love with club culture. His new loft, located in what had once been a 19th-century caviar factory, retains its original brick walls, timber columns, and wood windows, through which he can view slices of the Hudson River. A previous renovation had made smart use of the 2,500 square feet, carving out a primary suite, guest bedroom, office, powder room and pantry alongside the open cooking/living/dining space. It all just needed to be pared back. “The moment you take away everything, you have all you need,” Piqueras says.

Working with the Brazilian-born furniture and interior designer Pali Xisto Cornelsen, he stripped back what time-stamped interventions had been made over the years. In the kitchen, they updated the existing high-gloss kitchen cabinetry with white-painted fronts and chunky solid-cherry pulls, also installing stainless-steel countertops and a new island, trimmed in wood. The walls were coated in Benjamin Moore’s Simply White, the floorboards refinished, and the windows dressed in linen roman shades. “I was conscious of creating a neutral canvas,” says Xisto Cornelsen, who removed all the recessed lighting. “You’re gonna feel a certain calm.”

A David Wojnarowicz artwork hangs above a circa-1960 Knoll console.

The den features a built-in daybed; etchings by David Hockney and photograph by Nan Goldin.

Art introduces faces to that expanse. Working with advisor Joe Sheftel to expand his collection, Piqueras has assembled a sophisticated trove with a focus on works by Queer talents of recent or current memory. Those include photographs by Wolfgang Tillmans, Peter Hujar, and Alvin Baltrop, who documented the pre-AIDS gay revelry of the nearby Hudson River piers. Elsewhere are portraits by Larry Stanton and David Hockney. Some bare bodies, Piqueras admits, have left houseguests blushing. But the intention was never skin for the sake of shock. “It’s a lot about community,” says Sheftel. “The apartment also functions that way, as a fun space for friends and play.” A romantic spirit comes across in still lives (a burning candle by Phoebe Helander) and landscapes ( a Doron Langberg painting of Fire Island Pines). Evident too is Piqueras’s deep love of New York City. “There’s also a narrative of activism—of power and creativity through crisis,” says Sheftel, pointing out works by David Wojnarowicz.

In the dining area, Charlotte Perriand chairs surround a Pierre Chapo table beneath a Paavo Tynell lamp; photograph by Wolfgang Tillmans, still life by Phoebe Helander, and portrait by Larry Stanton.

Displayed above the custom DJ station (aka Piqueras’s little Berlin) are works by Wolfgang Tilmans, Seth Baker, and Issy Wood.

A Doron Langberg painting hangs amidst the kitchen’s reimagined cabinetry; photograph by Wolfgang Tillmans and stools by Alvar Aalto.

The library features a mix of vintage Scandinavian finds, including a Märta Blomstedt lounge chair, Paavo Tynell pendant light, and a desk and side chair by Axel Einar Hjorth. The large-scale photograph is by Wolfgang Tillmans and the shelves display works by Alvin Baltrop, David Wojnarowicz, Jacob Littlejohn, Peter Hujar, and Giangiacomo Rossetti. Resting on the floor is an etching by David Hockney.

A Hunter Reynolds artwork takes pride of place above Piqueras’s bed; speakers by Ojas.

The primary bath retains the building’s original brickwork.

Elsewhere throughout the interiors, they added custom millwork, including the office’s daybed and wall-mounted desk, the living area’s bookshelves, and the dining area’s DJ station, a corner Piqueras calls his little Berlin. Tapered silhouettes and bevels soften edges. “There are all these happy surprises,” says Cornelsen, who referenced design heroes like Le Corbusier, Joaquim Tenreiro, and Jean Prouvé. Vintage furniture adds to that neutral rhapsody, with choice finds by Pierre Chapo, Isamu Noguchi, and Alvar Aalto, whose coffee table prototype anchors the living area. It is joined by a cast of other Scandinavian characters, among them light fixtures by Paavo Tynell, the upholstered Märta Blomstedt lounge chair where Piqueras enjoys his morning tea, and pieces by Axel Einar Hjorth.

Collecting and decorating, Piqueras has found, are not unlike his daily profession. “Renovating an apartment is a kind of production,” he says. “My skill is to orchestrate.” But it’s a break from the grind that he now gets to relish at home. “Work is insane. The streets are insane. But then I can come here,” he says. “I put down my phone—and then I don’t think about it.”

A Paavo Tynell pendant crowns the guest bedroom, which features more custom millwork and displays artworks by Precious Okoyomon (left) and Christopher Culver.

A Wolfgang Tillmans photograph takes the place of the guest bath’s vanity mirror.

A Sol LeWitt artwork rests on the den’s custom desk; photograph by Wolfgang Tillmans and chair by Axel Einar Hjorth.

#4795. The 8 Best Weight Benches, Tested by Editors and Certified Trainers

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Expand your training possibilities at home with one of these picks.

A TRUE NECESSITY for any real home gym, a great weight bench opens the door to a ton of exercise possibilities. The best weight benches are sturdy and reliable, allowing you access to a whole range of exercises, and the ability to target nearly every muscle in your body.

The best weight benches can be used for way more than just the classics that bear its name, like the bench press. "They're good for everything from chest presses, dumbbell bench presses, incline bench supersets, skull crushers, glute bridges, incline rows to hit your back, ab moves, quad and leg moves like split squats, and more biceps moves than you can imagine," explains Men's Health Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, CSCS Neither flat nor adjustable weight benches occupy as much room as bulkier equipment, such as a hefty power rack, either. And for those that are adjustable, you can easily change the angle on your presses.

Whether you prefer to do your weight work with barbells or dumbbells (or even adjustable dumbbells), the best weight benches are compatible. Plus, many of the best weight benches include attachments and hidden features that allow for an even wider range of workouts, like a leg developer or squat rack.

We've gathered a selection of top-notch weight benches after rigorous testing and research to elevate your training and home gym experience. Keep reading, because you can't go wrong with any of these eight benches.

This model from Hammer Strength was originally introduced in 2016 exclusively for athletics and clubs, and was designed to be a versatile bench with an Olympic rack system. We're such a fan of this brand, we've got quite a few pieces in our own Men's Health gym. It's American-made and sold around the world due to its high-quality, durable construction.

With seven different back pad positions (from −10 degrees for decline lifts and up to 75 degrees for overhead presses), it packs more multi-functionality than most benches out there. Plus, it has built-in wheels, making it great for home gym spaces that require moving a bench around during workouts to accommodate space.

From Samuel's point of view, this is one of the sturdiest benches he's ever used. "Its tough surface lets me create a great base for bench presses," he says. An underrated thing he loves: the comfort of the seat portion of the bench, which allows for locking in a good position during overhead presses and incline curls.

It's more expensive than other options in this guide, but if you're looking for a bench that can keep up with your biggest reps and hardest lifts, this pick has got your back.

REP Fitness nailed it with this piece. This is the bench that I choose to lift with at home. The assembly is as easy as you could hope for with a heavy-duty bench like this. A few separate parts connect with screws and an Allen key. Everything was put together and ready for my workout in less than half an hour (just enough time for you to feel accomplished but not tired).

This bench shines in that it is as comfortable as it is durable. Few benches combine sturdiness, comfort, and versatility like this one from REP Fitness. It offers six different incline angles and a three-post design that anchors it to the floor no matter the exercise. It can also support up to 1,000 pounds, making it a solid option for novice to intermediate lifters.

"The backrest feels way more cushioned than other benches in its class, yet still manages to deliver rigidity when I drive my shoulder blades down for a set of bench presses," explains Samuel. This bench has only a minimal gap between the seat and back, which has never interfered with any of our lifts. It's also not ridiculously heavy (less than 100 pounds), so it's easy to move around my home gym when needed.

It's also a total breeze to adjust from fully flat up to a 90-degree incline. I've never had an issue with either of the two adjustment mechanisms getting stuck. Three seat positions add to its versatility, too. And the roller pads help secure your lower body with decline sit-ups and decline presses.

Read More: Our REP Fitness AB-3000 Review

Bowflex's flagship 5.1S Collapsible Bench is a good mid-range weight bench for small spaces and beginners. What we love most about this bench is its stowable design—when not in use, it can be stored vertically to reduce its footprint by more than 50 percent. For those who only use a bench at home from time to time and aren't pushing hundreds of pounds per exercise, this transformable option is a great choice.

"This bench is rated to support up to 600 pounds, but keep in mind that it's considerably lightweight," says Samuel. "Meaning if you line up on there for, say, incline rows or preacher curls, it may slip. I find it works best for me for bench presses and seated exercises like press, biceps curls, etc."

The position of the leg bar is not perfect, especially for those moving heavy weight, and we found it can act as a roadblock to setting up lifts properly. That being said, there is a good number of exercises that you can do properly with this bench not possible with others. It features six adjustable settings, including 30, 45, 60, 90 degrees, flat, and more decline range than most similar benches we've tested (−20 degrees).

Flat benches often support more weight than their adjustable counterparts, but the REP Fitness FB-3000 tops the charts with the best weight capacity and comfort features of any flat bench we've tested. Grippy vinyl upholstery prevents slippage on its surface when setting up for a lift, and firm, high-density foam cushioning makes driving down feel as stable as benches double its price. There's even an optional wall hanger for stowing it away when not in use.

It stands 17 inches from the floor to the top of the pad, and features a three-post design equipped with wheels and a handle to make moving it around easy. Its dimensions are largely consistent with benches used in powerlifting competitions, ensuring powerlifting users a training experience that closely aligns with professional standards. Talk about setting up for success, right?

"For less than $200, there isn't a better flat bench on the market. Especially for simple, foundational lifts like the bench press," explains Thorp. "I'm a big fan of how simple this bench is, with even padding throughout, making it a solid option for weighted step-ups as well."

The FB-3000 distinguishes itself with incredible value, but it does come with the same limitations as any flat bench: You miss out on a range of exercises that incline positions on adjustable benches provide. A flat bench is great for most powerlifters, but limiting to the rest of us lifting at home. Beyond its performance, this flat bench comes in various colors, including glossy black, red, blue, and textured versions, allowing users to personalize their gym setup.

Following extensive testing over the years, we've determined this bench to be the most versatile, and a standout in this guide of solid choices, which is why it made our Men’s Health Fitness Awards. This adjustable bench from Prime Fitness USA earned its spot primarily due to its stability—unlike lighter benches, it stays put during exercises on nearly any surface we've tested. Boasting a weight capacity of 1,000 pounds when flat and 600 pounds in an incline position, it can handle substantial weights for various fitness levels.

Seven adjustable backrest positions provide more flexibility than most benches, and the cushioning strikes a perfect balance between comfort and stability. The bench's quick switch between incline settings is also ultra smooth and efficient. Our Fitness Director Samuel enjoys this piece so much he wishes it was an option in the commercial gyms he frequents.

Heavy lifters will love how immovable this bench is: Unlike some lighter benches, it won’t slide away from you with exercises like chest-supported rows—regardless of the surface. With the substantial weight capacity, we felt confident and stable pushing heavy weight on this bench. The trade-off is that it's heavy itself, and while it has built-in wheels for transport, we wouldn't plan on taking it up and down the stairs a lot.

The cushioning manages to be comfortable while still providing a stable, sturdy base. Speaking of bases, the footprint on this bench is more sizable than most, so consider dimensions carefully if you're tight on space.

For those in search of a better-looking bench fit for your living room or guest room, this new offering from Matrix is a great option. The build is commercial-grade, and fit for most heavy lifts. This bench is part of a set the manufacturer offers that includes adjustable dumbbells and a storage rack, for those who are seeking a sleek-looking package.

"I like how easy it is to move and store this bench for how stable and sturdy it is," says Thorp. "Combined with the adjustable dumbbells, it brings everything that I need for a solid workout to my basement, with an aesthetic that elevates the room."

As sturdy as the bench is, it lacks the weight capacity of the Prime or the Hammer Strength benches. Able to handle up to 650 pounds, it should withstand the majority of training scenarios, but if you're a bodybuilder looking to move some real weight, there are probably better places to look in this guide.

The versatility of this bench is another highlight, with five different angles of incline and the ability to reverse the backpad to better support individuals with different body types or other comfort demands. The wheels and handle make it easy to move, and storing against the wall for additional floor space is simple.

This flat bench from Flybird is a suitable option for beginners who are tight on space, offering good value at right around $100. While there are higher-quality flat benches available at a higher price point, the foldable legs make it a standout choice for storage when not in use. The pin and lock system for the folding legs is efficient, taking less than a minute to set up or break down.

The bench is also extremely lightweight, making it easy to move and store as needed. However, for those performing lifts with dumbbells over 50 pounds, a heavier option is preferable for more stability. Despite its lightness, we found it reliable for various exercises like light dumbbell presses, curls, and skullcrushers at home.

According to Samuel, this is a very solid entry-level bench. "It's more on the cushioned side and actually very comfortable," he explains. "It's obviously not going to do incline and is prone to sliding, so you definitely want a yoga mat under it." It's a budget-friendly option suitable for novice and intermediate lifters, as long as precautions are taken to stabilize the bench.

This bench has become Amazon’s top-selling option because it comes almost fully assembled and seems easy to store. It isn’t the lightest option out there but, for the bench’s advertised versatility, the weight isn’t too bad and it folds up neatly.

We have reservations about this bench though, as it isn’t as stable as it appears—while having a 660-pound capacity, that doesn’t mean you can count on security for all of the movements you might do with it. The padding separation that makes it possible to fold may cause some discomfort when doing decline presses or sit-ups.

While it won’t be at the top of our recommendations for serious lifters (it will shift on you), it seems to be a decent budget option for beginners who aren’t sure how much they’re going to spend on home gym equipment. Though there is a little added peace of mind coming at the hands of Amazon’s classification, indicating that it’s a product “customers usually keep.”

First and foremost, you'll need a weight bench strong enough to handle your training regimen—and even if you're not doing heavyweight moves, you'll want it to support a decent amount of load. That's because it's about more than your bodyweight and the weight you're training with; each time you set up on the bench, there's potential for additional impact. In general, aim for a bench that can support at least 500 pounds; that'll set you up for success in nearly all your training and support more advanced exercises that bring even more impact (such as step-ups and plyometric Bulgarians).

The right balance between stiff and cushioned padding is essential to ensure your bench will stay in good condition with use. Highly cushioned benches might feel nice, but they tend to deform over time, creating an uneven surface. This can also compromise your form during workouts, especially when your spine or shoulders are required to stay in alignment. While most padding is stitched to the bench, some is stapled, which tends to lift away from the bench’s frame eventually. Not enough padding isn't good either, as you'll feel like you're lying on a plywood board.

If you plan on using your adjustable bench for flat bench variations, be mindful of the distance between the back pad and seat pad (otherwise known as the ‘pad gap’). Anything larger than 2 inches will be noticeable and may feel uncomfortable during certain lifts.

In general, the three types of weight benches are flat, adjustable incline, and adjustable incline/decline. The first two are pretty self-explanatory and the latter, of course, adds versatility for decline-angle exercises. "If you're unsure which bench to get, opt for a bench with incline-angle options. Sure, this may cost slightly more initially, but it'll set you up with a bench that can grow with you," explains Samuel. "In general, most website workouts and app workouts assume that, if you're training with a bench, it has incline options. So not having incline options can set you up for frustration. It'll also heavily limit your ability to vary your workouts in fun ways. The incline bench is the most future-proofed purchase option."

If you're a powerlifter, or you're buying a bench for a particular program, a flat bench might be perfect. Decline-angle benches open up new movements (especially when it comes to core training), but they're generally unnecessary. Think of that as your luxury option.

Like all home gym equipment, weight benches can take up a lot of room. If you’re tight on space or just appreciate being able to move your equipment out of the way, consider a collapsible weight bench or, at the very least, one with wheels. If you’re after an adjustable weight bench, wheels should be a top priority. Because they’re on the heavier side, this will make stowing away and setting up tremendously easier. You don't want setting up your bench every session to be a part of your workout.

Return policies and warranties represent the manufacturer’s confidence in its product. And with most home gym equipment manufacturers, the better the quality, the better the warranty. In the case that something goes wrong with your bench, it’s important to know your investment is protected, so look for benches that come with at least a one-year warranty.

As the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, my job is to evaluate the latest and greatest training equipment available. I've had extensive experience with weight benches in both the training facilities I've worked out of and the home gyms I've built. I also consulted with Men's Health fitness experts, editors, and writers on the top weight benches they’ve experienced firsthand. The experts included our own Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. and Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM. The team has tested dozens of weight benches over the years, from high-end, commercial-grade models to budget options.

Our extensive testing process involved a comprehensive evaluation of multiple factors—including size, durability, performance, suitability for different fitness levels, and value—to ensure that we recommend only the best. We tested each weight bench through exercise routines that included flat and adjustable bench moves, covering a wide range of motions and use scenarios. To determine stability and structural integrity, we tested benches at both comfortable and near-maximum capacities, allowing us to assess performance under varying loads.

To gather diverse perspectives, we consulted with our MH Advisory Board and Strength in Diversity trainers, who provided valuable feedback on the top weight benches based on their expertise and experiences. The result is the picks for the best weight benches you can buy right now.

You don’t necessarily need a weight bench to get strong and build muscle, but having one gives you access to a host of exercises (regardless of fitness level), especially when it comes to upper-body training.

Most basic exercises that beginners should master, like dumbbell presses and single-arm dumbbell rows and hip thrusts, are much easier to execute with a bench (especially an adjustable one). Meanwhile, more advanced lifters can get incredible mileage out of a bench by unlocking more innovative moves like half-bench single-arm presses and single-arm rows.

Here's a breakdown of the key differences:

A flat weight bench is designed with a fixed, flat surface, whereas an adjustable weight bench allows you to adjust the angle of the bench to different incline or, in some cases, decline angles.

"The adjustable benches that offer a decline setting are a terrific value for anyone who wants to get creative with their core exercises while training at home," says Samuel.

"Adjustable benches give you so many more options for your exercises," explains David Otey, C.S.C.S and Men's Health Advisory Board member. "Instead of just working at flat or upright, all of the angles in between can give you variety and diversity in your training options." Those angles allow you to bias muscle groups in different, more selective ways. A flat weight bench limits you to exercises that can be performed on a flat surface.

Adjustable benches offer more convenience overall (especially well-built ones), offering access to more movements and angles. Adjustable benches also offer support for extra movements, such as overhead presses and lateral raises, which can allow for greater loading of those movements in the long term. But flat weight benches win for convenience in two areas. They're generally lighter, so you can more easily move them around your gym, and they're easier to stow when not in use, too.

Because flat weight benches generally have fewer mechanisms and lack a hinge of any sort, they'll be easier to maintain. Adjustable benches don't require a ton of maintenance, but it's worthwhile every so often to check on bolts and caps, and make sure your hinge mechanism is working smoothly.

We consulted with Men's Health Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., for the best exercises for beginners to get the most out of a weight bench.

Charles Thorp is the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, where he shares the best product recommendations in gym equipment, recovery tools, supplements, and more. Following an early life in athletics, Charles became a NASM-certified trainer and began writing programs alongside the most respected coaches in the world.   Since entering the world of fitness content, Charles has had the opportunity to learn from and train alongside high performance individuals from the NFL, UFC, NBA, Formula 1, CrossFit, US Olympics, and Navy SEALs. When he’s not writing about training programs or gear, he can be seen at the gym or in the wild, putting them to the test.

Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., is the fitness director of Men's Health and a certified trainer with more than 10 years of training experience. He's logged training time with NFL athletes and track athletes and his current training regimen includes weight training, HIIT conditioning, and yoga. Before joining Men's Health, he served as a sports columnist and tech columnist for the New York Daily News.

Now, there’s nothing wrong with a position that consistently helps you orgasm. While trying out new sex positions can certainly help you climax, novelty also produces feel-good hormones that benefit your overall health. #4793. Why Gratitude Sometimes Backfires

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

You can appreciate the people in your life and still dread being asked to announce it over dinner.

The turkey is carved. The cranberry sauce has made its annual appearance in the shape of the can it came from. Then someone says: “Let’s go around the table and say what we’re grateful for.”

Forks pause midair. Eyes drift toward the mashed potatoes like they might offer an escape.

A cousin says something heartfelt and beautiful, and now the emotional bar has been raised to Olympic height.

Am I grateful enough? Should I say something profound?

Gratitude rituals are meant to create warmth. And often they do. But psychologically, gratitude is a little more complicated than the greeting cards suggest.

The benefits are real. A 2023 meta-analysis of 25 randomized controlled trials involving 6,745 participants found that expressing gratitude reliably improved happiness, life satisfaction, and psychological well-being compared with neutral activities.

But that doesn’t tell us everything about how gratitude feels in the moment.

In three experiments, psychologists examined people’s feelings after exercises such as recalling another person’s kindness or writing a gratitude letter they never sent. Alongside feeling moved and uplifted, the gratitude participants tended to report more indebtedness (and sometimes more feelings of guilt) than participants who did a neutral task.

It's like unwrapping a gift and realizing you didn’t bring one.

Gratitude can feel uplifting and slightly uncomfortable at the same time. It can carry a kind of social math: They gave + I received = Now I owe them

That discomfort doesn’t necessarily mean something has gone wrong. Wanting to give something back can be part of caring for a relationship.

But if gratitude can make us feel both good and uncomfortable, what happens when the discomfort arrives from somewhere else entirely?

In a randomized study of 156 undergraduates, participants completed about 12 minutes of gratitude practice, mindful breath awareness, loving-kindness, or a neutral visualization exercise. Those who practiced gratitude did report more positive emotion.

But then researchers introduced a stressor: Participants had to submerge their hand in a bucket of ice-cold water while a researcher in a lab coat stood nearby, observing with the emotional warmth of a marble statue — which is exactly as pleasant as it sounds.

Under that stress, the gratitude group actually became the most emotionally reactive, reporting more negative emotion than any of the other groups. And of the four groups, they were also the least likely to donate time to help others afterward.

Does this mean we should cancel giving thanks? Of course not.

Gratitude strengthens relationships and reinforces others’ kindness. But there's a difference between privately reflecting on gratitude and sharing it.

Privately reflecting on someone's kindness can leave us with an emotional mix: appreciation, plus obligation. Expressing gratitude may not make those complicated feelings disappear. But it can offer something more: connection.

A study of 916 students compared four approaches: writing gratitude letters they never sent, sending personal thank-you texts, posting gratitude publicly on social media, or just tracking daily activities. Participants repeated their assigned activity four times over about a week. Those who sent personal thank-you texts showed the strongest gains in feeling connected to and supported by others.

The takeaway isn't that texting is magical. It's that gratitude may do more to strengthen feelings of being connected and supported when we share it directly with the person we're grateful for rather than keeping it to ourselves.

And it may mean more to that person than we realize. In experiments by Amit Kumar and Nicholas Epley, people expressing gratitude underestimated how positive recipients would feel and overestimated how awkward they would feel.

The thank-you you’re second-guessing may land more warmly than you expect.

In my book, Micropractice: A Science-Backed Approach for Calm, Clarity, and Joy in 30 Seconds or Less, I explore in greater depth how to practice gratitude without getting caught in feelings of indebtedness, and how to weave more appreciation, connection, and joy into the moments you already have.

This Thanksgiving, when you feel gratitude for someone, try expressing it to them. Here’s a simple trick: Put a “you” in the sentence.

Instead of, “I’m grateful for my family," try, “Mom, you’ve always made people feel at home, even when the turkey’s running late.”

Instead of, “I’m grateful for my friends," try, "Noor, you’re the person I call when life gets messy, and somehow you always have a way of making it lighter.”

One describes what matters to you. The other lets someone know they matter.

Gratitude isn’t just noticing goodness. It’s letting someone know they helped create it.

This Thanksgiving, don’t just count your blessings. Let your blessings know they’re counted.

#4792. 16 Best Wallpaper Brands to Transform a Room (2026): Editor Picks

Shopping for wallpaper is an excellent way to discover just how indecisive you can be. Between painterly florals, graphic stripes, and whimsical prints, narrowing down the options is practically a full-time job. And that's before you get into the textures, finishes, and the peel-and-stick versus traditional wallpaper debate. There's a pattern for just about every room, taste, and level of commitment. Luckily, we've done some of the research for you.

Wallpaper can also do a lot more than cover four walls. A scenic mural can feel more like large-scale art, and built-in bookshelves can get a refresh simply by lining their backs. Even a drawer lined with your favorite print can be a delightful little surprise, not to mention a low-stakes project for a first-time DIYer. Whether you're ready to commit to an entire room or just want to test the waters, these are the wallpaper brands worth adding to your Pinterest board.

Spin through Spoonflower’s assortment of designs if you’re looking for more impactful wallpaper options. Thanks to graphic designer collaborations with independent artists, this wallpaper catalog includes unexpected patterns (some with a sense of humor!). You’ll also find more traditional floral and graphic patterns, including dreamy prints that hark back to the days of the Great Gatsby.

Consider these pinstripes a subtle way to showcase your team loyalty. This print suits any number of installation methods, whether you prefer peel-and-stick, pre-pasted rolls, vinyl, or grasscloth. There are even metallic accents you can choose for added glamour.

A geometric print awakens a space in a jiffy, and these Bauhaus circles are prime for a midcentury modern abode. Picture it surrounding a fireplace mantle or in an entryway. Adding the print to a ceiling is an unexpected move that gives the space a wow factor.

Wayfair doesn’t miss a thing—hidden amongst their enormous catalog of affordable furniture and decor is a considerable collection of wallpaper. Every print and pattern under the sun is represented here, from chevron to toile to florals.

This tile-inspired temporary wallpaper can work as a backsplash for a “blah” kitchen, on the walls surrounding your soaking tub, or as panels on cabinets. The tiles have a crisp look and, honestly, look pretty close to the real deal.

When in doubt, toile it out. Toile patterns are an easy way to introduce elevated detail. Their classic, subtle details keep things simple, but dynamic. Plus, they work in many different spaces—a bedroom (child or adult), a bathroom, a backsplash, or a living room decorated with early Baroque pieces.

Serena & Lily offers a small, curated collection of nautical, floral, and patterned designs (many that include natural elements like hydrangeas, palm leaves, and sea shells) for dressing up a nursery or bedroom. The color palettes tend to be soft blues, beiges, and variegated greens that play up to the coastal aesthetic.

For Wedgwood fans, this antique-style print is a serene surprise. (Just keep in mind that it’s not removable before taking on a full project.) Pro tip: The brand recommends using a wallpaper liner if you’re working with uneven wall surfaces to keep the finished project smooth.

Here’s another understated option with subtle texture, available in pastels like pistachio, sand, and sky. The muted tones make a great backdrop to any design style, lending the whole room a sense of calm.

While browsing for furniture, we stumbled upon Anthropologie’s robust collection of elevated wallpaper designs that span sophisticated florals and chinoiserie, damasks, and truly special geometric patterns. Their knack for hand-block prints, Renaissance revival, and arabesque designs makes them a no-brainer for any room that you want to be an absolute showstopper. Don’t sleep on their wall murals, too.)

Green bedrooms are trending, but if you want to up the ante on the soothing factor, look no further than this dreamy chinoiserie mural with cerulean-feathered songbirds and lemons to give your space a bit of joie de vivre.

Showcasing Southern artist Jordan Connelly's signature painterly style, these repeating seashells are a non-cliché way to bring a coastal feel to your space. Plus, the tonal color palette makes this great for a child's bedroom or bathroom.

For subtle stripes and vintage-inspired botanicals, McGee & Co.’s small-but-mighty wallpaper selection is there to fulfill your elevated farmhouse needs. Designed to perfectly suit her existing selection of furniture and decor, McGee’s wallpaper serves as a statement finishing touch, one you soon wouldn’t be able to envision your hallway or powder room without. You’ll even find her take on antique Morris and Co. florals through her pastel-hued collaboration.

This moody floral is ideal for crafting a cozy corner in a bedroom or den, especially in the navy colorway. Pair with the matching throw pillows for a pattern-drenching moment.

Sometimes all it takes is a simple stripe to elevate your space. Thanks to its neutral colorway, you can liven it up or tone it down to your heart's content with a blend of upholstery tones, artwork, and decor. Treat it like paint, just with a bit more oomph.

Chasing Paper is our go-to when we want something elevated that has a dash of whimsy. The brand is known for designer collaborations, too. Most recently, Fariha Nasir translated the South Asian art of block printing into wallpaper with floral garlands and tapestry-like designs. All Chasing Paper patterns come in four options: faux grasscloth, performance vinyl, peel-and-stick, and traditional paper. While we checked out samples in all materials, we can vouch for the durability and crisp pattern of peel-and-stick. They also offer tile decals (that happen to work as contact paper to upgrade worn countertops.)

As far as peel-and-stick wallpapers go, the self-adhesive poly-woven fabric of Chasing Paper is second to none. “I am no stranger to putting up peel-and-stick and the Peonies pattern I used for my home office is on par with luxe wallcoverings for heritage brands,” says contributor Yelena Alpert. “The paper adhered securely to the wood paneling, but it had no trouble coming up if I had to realign a panel. The best part is that I did not get any air bubbles—it’s a DIY miracle.” While Alpert opted for the bold red-and-grey colorway that reminded her of Diana Vreeland’s crimson interiors, a toned-down gold-and-cream is also available.

For fans of cabana stripes, this design from Chasing Paper agrees with minimalists and maximalists alike. It’s tough to choose between seven colorways (though we are partial to daisy yellow), which are all great for different purposes: mud rooms, nurseries, beachy bathrooms, or a design-forward living room.

The contemporary meets midcentury aesthetic of West Elm seamlessly carries through to their wallpaper collection, which includes fetching grasscloth designs and designer collaborations, like their latest with design studio Pierce & Ward. Patterns are geometric and playful but not kitschy, and work perfectly for accent walls. You can also find a few animal print designs and artsy figure drawings that are suitable for powder rooms.

Add this organic, playful peel-and-stick wallpaper to your wish list. Those who aren’t homeowners will love how easy the cleanup is for removable wallpaper when moving day rolls around. And when it comes to wallpaper motifs, simple is sometimes better—the soothing neutrals and distinct geometric pattern will elevate and simultaneously calm any room or nook.

Let’s say you want something neutral and textured but grasscloth is not your cup of tea. The Piece & Ward Floral Lattice design is a worthy alternative as it gives the wall a 3D moment but won’t compete with furnishings, especially if you’re into warm wooden pieces. Include ceramic pieces in your home decor to give the entire space a layered look.

The celebrated 19th century British designer, William Morris, was a traditionalist devoted to his craft in the midst of the Industrial Revolution. He taught himself block printing techniques to create more than 20 nature-inspired patterns that encapsulate the Arts & Crafts Movement. His design brand Morris & Co. was established in 1861 and has shown no signs of slowing down as contemporary designers continue to incorporate the wallpaper patterns in their projects. Each wallpaper design is batch-printed in the United Kingdom, making it a good practice to order all rolls at the same time to ensure the dye lots are the same.

The Strawberry Thief is one of Morris & Co.’s most popular patterns and was inspired by the birds that would pop into Kelmscott Manor, Morris’s home in Oxfordshire, to steal the berries from the kitchen. “The gravure printed paper has this heirloom quality that makes it feel as if it is directly plucked from the archives,” says contributor Yelena Alpert, who has samples in indigo and crimson colorways. “Each cheeky bird is about the size of my hand, and the foliage has this watercolor quality. It would look amazing above wood paneling, painted or not.”

Part of the Morris & Co., pattern appeal is that each floral motif is actually on a grid, giving it a certain rhythm. Pimpernel, another favorite, is ornate in the way that the swirls repeat without overwhelming the eye. This design is seen in the Kelmscott House dining room and was chosen by Morris himself. It comes in 16 colorways that span blues, greens, and venture into burgundy.

More than just a place to find scalloped accent chairs and fashion-inspired collaborations (Aimee Song and Carly Cushnie, anyone?), Lulu & Georgia also offers wallpaper. Of course, you can find the likes of Morris & Co. and Scalamandre, but the brand also has their own in-house line. Design stars Sarah Sherman Samuel and Jake Arnold have also lent their talents to this stock with luxe grasscloths and ornate botanicals. Here you’ll find perfect pairings for your velvet bed frame or curved sofa.

Designed by Sarah Sherman Samuel, this intricate print is made more luxe with the addition of a subtle paper weave, adding texture to the linework style drawings.

Polka dots are a playful addition to standard pinstripes, creating a whimsical gateway for those more inclined to traditional styles of design.

Beloved for their quirky paint color names like Disco Nap (a pale acid yellow) and Silver Lake Dad (a stormy blue grey), Backdrop Home also makes patterned wallcoverings that perfectly color-match their hues. Once absorbed into Schumacher’s family of brands, Backdrop also launched archival prints, textured sisal, and peel-and-stick wallpaper options. Backdrop Home offers the kind of whimsical designs that you can’t find elsewhere. Swirling snakes and quilt-like geometric prints that instantly liven up any room, and will have you saying, ‘Oh yeah, that’s Backdrop.’

Taken from the archives of fabric brand Schumacher, Backdrop Home’s iteration takes notes from John Groth’s original 1957 fabric. The sketched horses and riders pair perfectly with the aptly named Ghost Ranch, a warm terracotta-esque brown.

Available in both sisal and plainweave, this geometric print becomes more subtle the more square footage you stretch it across. While wholly impactful in tight spaces like a closet or powder room, this print transforms in large scale, becoming almost hypnotic with its various plum tones.

With a stock full of ornate prints and patterns inspired by historic European textiles, Transylvanian brand Mind the Gap has something for every design style. Heritage-style plaids for the sophisticated sit alongside Eastern-influenced Ikats and jungle motifs for the maximalist. There are also plenty of coordinating textiles if you prefer to pattern-drench your space.

Inspired by upholstery textiles, this maximalist stripe gives the look of fabric-covered walls without the need for a specialty installation.

Vibrant and eclectic, this floral tapestry-style wallcovering recalls early Germanic florals and the brand founders’ childhoods in Transylvania.

York knows wallpaper. The wallcoverings producer has been around for more than 100 years and still dips into the archive to bring back designs from the early 18th century. The Susquehanna Valley, Pennsylvania, factory is the oldest and largest wallcovering producer in the United States. Even if you’re not into heirloom patterns, their designer series includes collections from Magnolia Home, Rifle Paper Co., Missoni, and LoveShackFancy, among many others.

The Italian knitwear company Missoni is now accessible to the more budget-conscious clientele with its new premium peel-and-stick collection (which also includes the iconic zigzags and florals). The Fireworks pattern is almost like a non-dizzying version of the 1990s Magic Eye motif. “I just ordered all three colorways—natural, mauve, and warm grey—to help me decide which one would look best as an accent wall behind my bed,” Alpert says. “Even though it is peel-and-stick, the texture is that of real wallpaper—smooth and velvety!”

A tonal geometric print adds just enough visual interest without overwhelming the eye. This print was designed by Joanna Gaines and the Magnolia Home team to combine the beauty of an artist's sketch with the structure of a true geometric pattern.

Boutique wallpaper brand Hygge & West are beloved for their colorful takes on botanicals and geometric patterns. With best sellers like the Alpine Garden and Bloom, the brand seems to have expertly mastered the ability to create visually striking designs that never overwhelm your space, no matter how small. Even in a powder room, the motifs draw the eye in just the right way, complementing your space instead of taking it over. However, if you’re a maximalist, there are definitely patterns for you too.

The Arcade print blends Pac-Man-like shapes and transforms them into a repeat that’s not dissimilar from a quilt block.

One of the brand’s best-sellers, Alpine Garden’s colors pop against the black background that adds a bit of moodiness to typically saccharine florals.

Not every home comes with a century's worth of character, but that doesn't mean it can't look the part. Best known for its period-inspired lighting and hardware, Rejuvenation brings that same appreciation for Old-World charm to its wallpaper collection. Think intricate botanicals, heritage-inspired prints, and textural takes on grasscloth and sisal that make even a new build feel storied.

Sisal doesn't have to stay underfoot. This Hoffmann print recreates the natural, woven texture in a peel-and-stick wallpaper, bringing instant warmth and dimension to the room.

The soft blue-and-cream palette keeps the Fencott print's small-scale leaf motif from feeling too busy.

Are you more drawn to the cozy, muted tones of winter or the vibrant colors of summer? At Claret & Key, you can have your favorite season on your walls year-round. The brand offers its wallpaper patterns in four seasonal color palettes, each giving the same design a different personality. And if none feels quite right, you can dip into the brand's extensive color library to create a combination of your own. Designs are also available in traditional, heavy-grade, and removable options.

Romeo's hand-drawn leaves give you the look of a custom mural without having to hire an actual muralist. The trailing foliage gives the walls a sense of movement, making this an especially fitting choice for a reading nook straight out of an English country house.

Nellie, on the other hand, brings a little sunshine to the nursery or kid’s room with its vintage-inspired lemon print. The Spring palette reads more neutral, with subdued tones that keep the citrus motif from feeling too playful.

Hang that framed landscape elsewhere—your walls deserve a full view. Crate & Barrel's scenic wallpaper murals turn blank walls into sprawling gardens and leafy landscapes that look as though an artist painted them right onto the surface. Its exclusive wallpaper collection is designed in-house and made in the USA by York Wallcoverings, with plenty of stripes, florals, and textured designs for those who prefer something more understated. If you're having trouble deciding, up to 10 free wallpaper samples should help narrow the field.

There's a reason Jardin has all the charm of a hand-painted landscape—it originally started as one. Painted in watercolor on canvas paper, the tree-lined scene was digitally scanned to preserve every brushstroke and subtle shift in color. The result is a dreamy, softly layered landscape that gives your walls the look of an original watercolor.

Vivaldi puts a wallpaper spin on the classic verdure tapestry. Printed on natural sisal, it even has the texture to play the part.

#4791. Ivy Shapiro's Manhattan Home is an Artful Ode to Old-School New York

Describing the allure of her sprawling prewar Manhattan apartment, art adviser Ivy Shapiro returns to one theme again and again. “It’s old-school,” she insists. “I have this fantasy that I’m living in a different era. I wanted the apartment to capture this nostalgic vision of old-school New York elegance.” She had plenty to work with. The bones of the unit—its high ceilings, architectural details, and idiosyncratic layout of generous salons and small, meandering rooms—remained largely intact. Major structural alterations were unnecessary to make the space her own, a home that reflects her singular character while graciously accommodating an extensive collection of art that ranges from Stone Age tools and Southeast Asian antiquities to modern and contemporary works created by friends and family.

A Joel Shapiro sculpture holds a corner of the dining room beneath a painting by Aubrey Saget. Works on paper by Edgar Degas and Bob Thompson surmount the fireplace, which is clad in black encaustic tile by clé.

In the living room, a painting by Cecily Brown hangs above a Joel Shapiro table with sculptures by Jonathan Borofsky (left) and Ivy Shapiro’s daughter, Lily Crewdson (right), beside a Southeast Asian sculpture. A Jasper Johns lithograph hangs at rear. Sculpture in foreground by Tony Smith.

A Jeremy Anderson chandelier from Gallery Fumi crowns the makeup room. On the wall are works on paper by Cecily Brown.

Shapiro was born into the New York art world of the 1970s, when the artist and collector community had a far different complexion than that of today, a time before “the art world” meant “the art-fair world.” She is the daughter of the late celebrated sculptor Joel Shapiro and art educator Amy Snider, and the stepdaughter of artist Ellen Phelan. Hers is a life organized around and by art, so it is no surprise that the same would be true of her apartment. Here, art is offered the same sovereignty as the home’s human inhabitants, the freedom to take up space, require concessions, demand attention, and even, occasionally, to trip you up. It doesn’t have to fit in above a sofa or over a mantel, nor does it have to stand for something—taste, wealth, a movement, a generation. She accords each piece the independence to exist on its own terms, to be at home.

“I like hanging art in weird places where people don’t like to hang,” Shapiro says. “It’s not an intellectual exercise. It’s more intuitive.”

Architect Raffaella Bortoluzzi, Shapiro’s accomplice in the gentle transformation of the home, drew inspiration from her client’s unconventional sensibility. “I love that Ivy decided not to combine the small rooms and try to impose a more contemporary approach on how the spaces flow. We wanted to respect the historic character and maintain the eccentricities,” Bortoluzzi notes. “Our idea was that every room should have its own little story. We focused on light, playful treatments that in no way fight the original architecture.”

Floating tiled shelves in the kitchen display ceramics by Warren MacKenzie and Shio Kusaka and a small sculpture by Joel Shapiro.

The television room features paintings by Lothar Hempel (left) and Elizabeth Murray (right).

A Joel Shapiro drawing has pride of place in the bedroom of Ivy Shapiro’s son, Walker Crewdson. To the right are a drawing by Sol LeWitt and a Joel Shapiro print.

The television room, for example, is enrobed in aubergine Venetian plaster. The home office, covered in a crimson plaster, features shelves and drawer fronts finished with a surface treatment of crushed eggshells encased in epoxy. Bortoluzzi goosed the primary bath by sprinkling a handful of Piero Fornasetti tiles among a field of pearlescent, zellige-like ones. In Shapiro’s makeup room, ladylike pink plaster walls are amplified by an antique mirror, custom shoe closets with floral fabric behind the glass case fronts, and a sprightly Jeremy Anderson chandelier. “Ivy is very funny and feminine in her way,” the architect says. “The design speaks to those aspects of her personality.”

In the dining room, a Jean Arp collage is installed above an antique tansu with Stone Age tools and Joel Shapiro maquettes.

The last sculpture Joel Shapiro created rests on a table in the primary bedroom. The painting is by Bob Thompson. The sofa is covered in a Rubelli brocade.

Shelves and drawer fronts in the home office are covered in a surface material of crushed eggshells by Nature Squared.

Within the newly refurbished architectural shell, Shapiro deployed her estimable collection of art and objets de vertu with wit and verve. In the living room, the way that Jonathan Borofsky’s bronze Split Head sculpture is balanced by the split-off stone head of an Asian deity feels like a call and response across the ages, as well as a vignette about the endurance of art. They flank a dynamic painting by Shapiro’s friend Cecily Brown like chaperones at an orgy of color and motion. A sculpture by Shapiro’s daughter, Lily Crewdson, joins the Borofsky piece atop a table made by her father, one of many Joel Shapiro sculptures, drawings, and maquettes installed throughout the apartment.

A sculpture by Richard Artschwager is installed above a Joel Shapiro bronze in a hallway.

An Axel Salto sculpture sits beneath an artwork by Ryan Sullivan in the living room.

In the hallway to the primary bedroom, a lyrical vintage Danish wall light of abstracted vines, leaves, and flowers hangs above a signature Carl Andre metal floor sculpture, the ultimate butch/femme pairing. In the bedroom itself, a sculpture that Joel Shapiro made in the hospital during his final days (he died in June of 2025) sits inconspicuously on a small table of his own design. It was the last artwork of his storied career.

“Living with so much of Joel’s art, and all these amazing things he and Ellen collected, connects me to [my dad],” Shapiro muses. “The way the apartment is set up, I feel like my life is completely integrated with the art.”

#4790. F1 Academy Is Coming to Apple TV, and Its Drivers Are Ready for Their Close-Up

The all-female racing series is getting a bigger platform in the U.S.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Starting in 2027, Apple TV will become the exclusive U.S. streaming home of F1 Academy, the all-female racing series developing the next generation of talent.

Fans will be able to watch every qualifying session and race on Apple TV, bringing more visibility to a series that is quickly gaining momentum. It also expands Apple's partnership with Formula 1, which began its five-year U.S. broadcast deal with the streaming service in 2026.

For Austrian driver Emma Felbermayr, who represents the Audi Revolut F1 team in F1 Academy, the announcement is particularly exciting.

“Apple TV is such a big platform, and it's all about F1 Academy getting more attention,” Felbermayr told Women's Health in Las Vegas ahead of the Grand Prix. “It just makes the interest into the sport much bigger, and that's what we need. We need to have more girls interested in the sport so that we get more attention. In the end, we want to get seen by people."

Launched in 2022, F1 Academy is a Formula 4-level development series designed to create more opportunities for women in motorsport. And its impact extends beyond the racetrack.

At a private dinner in Las Vegas celebrating the Apple TV announcement, F1 Academy managing director Susie Wolff reflected on the series' rapid rise.

“It's incredible how the sport has shifted in the last five to seven years,” Wolff said. “Women have a huge part to play in that shift, and that has been part of the reason why F1 Academy has had so much success in the short space of time.” The dinner event, co-hosted by Wolff and F1 Chief Commercial Officer Emily Prazer, brought together women from across the worlds of sports, entertainment, and advocacy, including activist Malala Yousafzai and model Kelly Piquet.

That growth is personal for Felbermayr, who says F1 Academy has helped her become more confident both in and out of the car. Once a self-described shy person, the 19-year-old has learned to navigate interviews, limited track time, and the pressure of competing at a high level.

“I got so much better in the language of English. That's maybe just a small part of it, but just getting more confident in front of the camera, but also in the car,” says Felbermayr, who just signed on for a third F1 Academy season with Audi. “Every challenge grows yourself as a person, and I think that's something I really saw in the last two years.”

With seven race weekends on the 2027 calendar, including stops in Austin and Las Vegas, American fans will have plenty of opportunities to get acquainted with F1 Academy's rising stars. And with Apple TV bringing their races to a wider audience, more young girls will have the chance to see what's possible behind the wheel.

2027 F1 Academy CalendarMarch 19-21: Jeddah Corniche Circuit, Saudi ArabiaApril 16-18: Shanghai International Circuit, ChinaMay 21-23: Circuit Gilles-Villeneuve, CanadaJuly 2-4: Silverstone Circuit, Great BritainJuly 30-August 1: Hungaroring, HungaryOctober 22-24: Circuit of The Americas, United StatesNovember 18-20: Las Vegas Strip Circuit, United States
