#4774. Tesla deemed liable for fraud after Solar Roof ‘experiment’ on a home

A California judge has deemed Tesla liable for fraud in a Solar Roof lawsuit, after the company repeatedly failed to hand over evidence. Tesla had already admitted it breached the contract, broke its warranty, and was negligent on the job.

The homeowner says fixing the damage will cost “well over $2.5 million.” Tesla once offered him $5,000.

The case is Conroy v. Tesla, filed in 2022 in San Diego Superior Court’s North County division (case No. 37-2022-00043670). Electrek reviewed the court orders, the complaint, and the parties’ joint trial readiness report. Here’s what’s in them.

Ambrose Conroy, who lives in Rancho Santa Fe, signed up for a Tesla Solar Roof in March 2020. The original contract was $82,210 for a 13.1 kW system. By February 2021, after two amendments, it had grown to roughly $110,000 for an 18.2 kW roof and six Powerwalls.

The roof was never finished. It never passed a county inspection, and it never produced a single kWh for the house.

Tesla isn’t contesting most of that anymore. In the joint report filed by both sides last month, Tesla stipulated to liability on three of the five claims.

The other two claims, fraud and negligent misrepresentation, are where things went badly for Tesla.

Judge Cynthia Freeland sanctioned Tesla twice over discovery before going further. She ordered it to pay $15,467.50 in February and another $13,500 in June, both times for failing to produce a proper privilege log and responsive documents, and both times warning that issue sanctions could follow.

Tesla missed the next deadline anyway. So on September 11, the court deemed Tesla liable for fraud and negligent misrepresentation, limiting the trial on those claims to compensatory and punitive damages.

The judge found “ample evidence to support that Defendants have acted willfully.” Among the missing records were Microsoft Teams messages (Tesla’s own corporate witness testified they’re kept “for infinity”), OSHA logs, emails with San Diego County inspectors, and more than 20 quality, install, and safety reports from Tesla’s internal Bolt system.

Tesla asked her to reconsider, arguing it had since produced everything. She said no in a ruling dated October 27, writing that the late documents could support Conroy’s theory that Tesla “knowingly used Plaintiff’s home as an experiment while knowing they lacked the experience to perform as promised.”

And the “experiment” word shows up in Tesla’s own messages, according to the trial exhibit list. Exhibit 224 is described as text messages from January 13, 2021, between Tesla’s director of model engineering Bobby Yang and other Tesla employees.

To be clear, that’s how Conroy’s side describes the messages on the exhibit list. We haven’t seen the texts themselves. But Elon Musk is on Conroy’s witness list, and internal emails quoted in the complaint point the same way.

On February 9, 2021, Yang wrote internally that the house was in the “99.5 percentile in terms of complexity” and that “if we can do this job well, we should be able to do any job well.” RJ Johnson, then head of Tesla’s energy business, replied that the project would “skew numbers” but that Tesla needed “to make it right.”

Johnson was fired in April 2021. The roof had at least 59 mounting planes, and one employee called it the largest job Tesla had attempted at the time, according to the complaint.

Conroy’s account of the installation reads like a list of everything that can go wrong on a roof. These are his allegations, but Tesla has now conceded breach and negligence.

The tear-off was supposed to take two days and took two weeks. Tesla left in November 2020 with bare roof decking exposed, then had crews work overtime on December 27 to get underlayment down before a storm. Tiles arrived scratched and damaged and went on the roof anyway. Glass tiles shattered in the driveway and lawn, and the family says they still can’t walk there barefoot.

By March 2021, Johnson had agreed in writing that paying “when you’re happy with the outcome is completely reasonable.” Tesla’s billing department kept calling anyway.

In August 2021, an internal email weighed just leaving.

The project went through at least seven project managers. In November 2021, Tesla told Conroy the people behind its repair plan were gone and it had nobody in the area to do the work.

In April 2022, Tesla offered $5,000 to settle everything.

It didn’t end there. In February 2025, more than two years into the lawsuit, Tesla failed another San Diego County inspection after showing up without the plans for the venting system. And this summer, Conroy’s electrical expert opened up part of the roof and concluded that the way Tesla ran wiring and conduit under the tiles created a short-circuit and fire risk in heavy rain. The roof is now coming off. Tesla’s lawyers point out that even Conroy’s counsel called that fire risk “counterintuitive.”

Tesla is fighting the sanction hard. In an October 29 filing, it asked the court to freeze the case while it petitions the California Court of Appeal, arguing the order is “unduly punitive,” violates due process, and amounts to a directed verdict on fraud before trial.

Tesla also says the discovery fight had no connection to the fraud claims and that it has now produced everything relevant. The judge already rejected that argument once.

The November 20 trial date is off. A trial readiness conference is set for December 4, and Conroy’s lawyers want to go to trial in December.

This isn’t the first Solar Roof horror story in this case file. Conroy’s complaint attaches our 2020 report on a Solar Roof buyer left with tarps over his house after Tesla tried an untested underlayment on his home. It also cites a 2025 California Contractors State License Board action seeking to revoke Tesla’s contractor licenses over abandoned Solar Roof jobs.

What a nightmare. This is the most damaging Solar Roof case I’ve seen, and I’ve been covering this product since Elon Musk unveiled it on a Universal Studios backlot in 2016.

A botched install isn’t news on its own. Tesla only installed about 3,000 of these roofs before killing the product this year, and plenty of them went sideways. What’s different here is the paper trail: internal emails calling a customer’s home a test of whether Tesla could do “any job,” texts describing the job as an “experiment” with daily reports going to Musk, and then years of Tesla failing to hand over its own records until a judge ran out of patience.

And Tesla’s response to all of it was $5,000.

Look, it’s normal for things not to go as planned with a new product, and early adopters need to be flexible. However, we are talking about someone’s literal roof over their head here and a trillion-dollar company. Tesla could have and should have made it right a long time ago.

Any time there are internal messages in the record that say essentially "let's skip town rather than try to make this right", it's a tough lift to make a jury think that everything was aboveboard.

The question that strikes me is whether this may also rise to the criminal level, since the CEO was apparently involved in the decision.

The issue sanction might not survive the Court of Appeal. Courts don’t love deciding fraud through discovery orders, and Tesla’s due process argument isn’t frivolous. But even if it gets reversed, Tesla has still admitted it breached the contract and was negligent, and the jury will see how this customer was treated.

This also says a lot about how Tesla ran the Solar Roof business. It sold a product it knew was hard to install, on homes it knew were complex, while the people running the program kept leaving. Conroy’s house was one of the worst cases, but installers are still dealing with the fallout of Tesla walking away from the product earlier this year.

The real question is what’s in those Teams messages and texts Tesla fought so hard to keep out of this case. If this goes to trial in December, we might find out.

Solar Roof was supposed to make going solar effortless. For most homeowners, conventional panels from a reputable local installer are the safer bet. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. And with lease and PPA options, you can do it with zero upfront cost and start saving immediately. If you want to find the best deal, check out EnergySage. It’s a free service with hundreds of pre-vetted installers competing for your business, so you save 20 to 30% compared to going it alone. No sales calls until you pick an installer. #4773. How to Not Lose Your Cool This Holiday Season

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

While the holidays can bring a great deal of joy, they can also trigger anger in a lot of people. Think having to face difficult people during annual social gatherings, being stuck in traffic or stranded at an airport because of delays, or feeling underappreciated for all the effort you’ve put into a holiday that others may not have acknowledged.

Anger is a powerful emotion. Chronically angry people are more likely to suffer from heart disease, diabetes, and impaired immune functioning. They're also more likely to have unhappy marriages, be lonelier, and struggle at work.

Anger itself is not the problem. It's a normal and healthy emotion like any other. But when it goes unchecked, it can make us do and say things that cause irreparable damage or act in ways we deeply regret.

To help you keep your cool this holiday season, here are five anger-management techniques you can start using—today.

Look around your surrounding environment and try to find five things that are blue. Alternatively, you can seek out five things that begin with the letter A. Either approach helps shift your attention from the source of anger to a neutral stimulus. This brief break helps you de-escalate through cognitive shifting by allowing your emotions to cool down. The more time we spend ruminating and focusing on what’s upsetting us, the more hotheaded we can become. Distraction techniques like these interrupt that anger-rumination-explosion cycle, reducing activity in the amygdala and allowing our heart rates and blood pressure to come back to baseline.

Inhale all the way. Hold your breath for three to four seconds. Exhale all the way (try to make your exhale longer than your inhale). Hold your breath again at the bottom of that exhale for another three to four seconds. Repeat several times until you feel a reduction in distress. This breathwork technique and others like it help regulate the nervous system by increasing activity within the parasympathetic nervous system—the branch of the autonomic nervous system undergirding resting and digesting functions—and downshifting activity within the sympathetic (fight/flight) nervous system.

When you feel yourself getting heated, try to imagine the anger you’re feeling as an object in your body. First, where is it? Then, what does it look like? Feel like? What’s its temperature and texture; its weight? Be as descriptive as you can. Then, take a deep breath in and, with that breath, imagine creating space around the object in your body. On the exhale, imagine breathing out its intensity—almost like you’re cooling off the object of anger in your body.

Many studies have found that mindfulness techniques such as this help to ease anger, in part by creating some distance between you and the anger itself, so that anger doesn’t take you on as great a roller coaster ride. Taking time to visualize and work with the emotion in the body also helps slow you down, so you don’t knee-jerked-ly blurt out something nasty or otherwise act impulsively in a way that may haunt you (and possibly ruin Thanksgiving dinner).

If you feel yourself starting to get worked up—you're gritting your teeth, your face is flushed, your breathing is shallow, your fists are clenched—see if you can excuse yourself to splash some very cold water on your face or hold some ice cubes to your chest or your temples. If you’re in a part of the world where it’s cold during the holiday season, go take a walk outside in the icy air. Exposure to very cold temperatures helps to trigger the diving reflex, which quickly lowers heart rate and can essentially shock your body back into a less elevated state.

This one is especially helpful for dealing with difficult people over the holidays. If you’re surrounded by folks who aren’t aligned with you politically, can be quite rude, or make unnecessary comments about your life, body, or any other personal aspect, imagine a force field around you. Really go deep with the visualization here. What color is the force field? What is it made of—ice? Fire? Laser beams? Does it make a noise? Then, imagine the difficult person’s (or persons’) statements bouncing off of the force field (better yet, if they make a funny noise when they do so), leaving you safe and protected. You can go the extra mile and imagine the statements bouncing back and tripping the other person, spilling all over them, or whatever other amusing visual will bring you more of a smile than a grimace.

All of these techniques can be useful in moments of high frustration leading to intense anger. (I use them with my clients, and also with myself.) If you find yourself becoming angry quite often or if you find it particularly challenging to de-escalate and not do things you later feel badly about, it may be worth connecting with a therapist who can help you practice skills like these as well as do some deeper work around the origins of any chronic anger you may be struggling with. Don’t hesitate to get help if this is the case. Your heart health will thank you if you do.

To find a therapist, please visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

#4772. What Poison Ivy Teaches Us About Environmental Grief

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

Poison Ivy may be the only Batman villain whose cause many readers quietly agree with.

In her origin story from Batman comics, Dr. Pamela Isley (Poison Ivy) was once a passionate scientist. However, she was injected with toxins that merged her with plant life. She can control vegetation and feel the pain of plants directly.1 Driven by empathic distress, she fights environmental abuse and political negligence. Archetypally, she embodies both the grief and the fury of a wounded Earth.

Her grief reflects emotions many of us share; the research literature captures how people commonly feel sadness, fear, anger, helplessness, and profound grief in response to ecological loss.2 This is closely tied to the experience of solastalgia, or the anguish of watching a cherished home environment deteriorate until it no longer offers the solace it once did.

Environmental grief and climate-related trauma are natural and instinctive responses to climate breakdown.3 They arise from tangible losses of ecosystems, wildlife, homes, jobs, and communities. They also arise from losses that are harder to see, such as diminished trust, a loss of faith in the future, and a deeper psycho-spiritual disconnection from Earth itself.

Poison Ivy is also a figure of political grief. She is driven by moral outrage at governance that permits deforestation, pollution, and the exploitation of the natural world. Environmental grief often intersects with political grief, especially as climate change and environmental breakdown places a far greater burden on disadvantaged communities and developing countries.4 Subsequently, growing numbers of people are questioning values that give personhood to corporations but not to the natural world.

Poison Ivy accurately shows how these losses can be felt on an intensely personal level, one that penetrates us to the core of our being.

Grief, hopelessness, and despair can push us into survival states marked by defensiveness, psychological inflexibility, and absolutist thinking.5 Over time, these experiences can lead people toward extremist positions, social alienation, and political polarization.6 Poison Ivy’s impulsive, destructive choices do not create meaningful collective change. Her over-identification with plants causes her to lose touch with her own humanity.

In troubling times, it can be tempting to imagine that we need a figure like Poison Ivy. This supervillain fantasy will not solve the ecological crisis, though, or meaningfully comfort our grieving hearts.

The world has already experienced enough destructive authoritarianism that violates all traditional cultural wisdom. Violence will only make problems worse, and coercion entrenches polarization and resistance.6 Tragically, supervillains embody the same cycles of harm they claim to oppose. Without an ethical framework, supervillains impose rigid ideologies that oppose cooperation, respect, dignity, and mutual understanding.

The environmental crisis and the ongoing tear in our political systems evoke a great deal of fear, which is exactly why we need superheroes. The Justice League from DC Comics is a diverse group of superheroes who unite against threats too large for any one of them to handle. Despite differing ideologies, they preserve a sense of common humanity.

Adopting a stance of common humanity does not require compromising deeply held values or excusing abuses of power.6 Instead, it means focusing on our intention to connect rather than our need to defend. Many Indigenous worldviews express this through four guiding values: relationship, responsibility, reciprocity, and redistribution.7

Over 40 years ago, Roger Walsh urged us to face collective existential threats from a place of psychological self-awareness rather than fear or shadow.8 External change is most effective when it is fuelled by inner transformation and by tending to our own unresolved losses. Furthermore, crises benefit from level-headed individuals who are respectful, strive to minimize harm, utilize ethical frameworks, and maintain unwavering integrity. In other words, people who can embody and psychologically integrate the qualities of a superhero are what the world needs.

When we can metabolize our widespread environmental and political grief, we create inner space and presence. That space awakens us to life, love, and interdependence, and to the ability to re-imagine the future. No one is also meant to face this grief alone. Our collective moment of reckoning has arrived, and we need all the superheroes we can muster.

This piece draws on my book chapter, “From Poison Ivy to the Justice League: A Psychological Approach to Environmental and Political Grief,” in Superhero Grief and the Multiverse of Loss: Considerations and Case Studies, edited by Jill Harrington and Darcy Harris (Routledge, 2026). This new collection uses superheroes and the multiverse to explore how non-death loss impacts our psychology.9

1. Tynion, J., & Ward, C. (2022). Batman secret files: The gardener. DC Comics.

2. Ágoston, C., Csaba, B., Nagy, B., Kőváry, Z., Dúll, A., Rácz, J., & Demetrovics, Z. (2022). Identifying types of eco-anxiety, eco-guilt, eco-grief, and eco-coping in a climate-sensitive population: A qualitative study. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 19(4), 2461.

3. Shelvock, M. (2023). What is ecological grief and trauma? Psychology Today.

4. Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (World Health Organization). (2023). Synthesis report: Summary for policymakers.

5. Shelvock, M., & Harris, D. (2024). Political grief. Psychology Today.

6. Harris, D. (2022). Political grief. Illness, Crisis & Loss, 30(3), 572-589.

7. Lent, J. (2022). The web of meaning: Integrating science and traditional wisdom to find our place in the universe. New Society Publishers.

8. Walsh, R. (1984). Staying alive: The psychology of human survival. New Science Library.

9. Shelvock, M. (2026). From Poison Ivy to the Justice League: A psychological approach to environmental and political grief. In J. Harrington & D. Harris (Eds.), Superhero grief and the multiverse of loss: Considerations and case studies (pp. 267-272). Routledge.
